guides/ABILITIES.html.summary: PlayForge — Abilities An Ability asset describes one thing an entity can do, such as a fireball, a dash or a heal. An entity is anything that runs a gameplay ability system (GAS), such as the player or an enemy. An entity learns an ability from its Entity asset's Starting Abilities, from an equipped Item, or from code (AbilitySystemComponent.GiveAbility). It keeps the ability until the ability is removed. Each time the ability activates, the GAS checks that it may run, lets a targeting task pick a target, then runs the ability's stages of tasks. The ability's cost and cooldown are gameplay effects, assets that change an entity, which it applies to its caster. Abilities run as processes under ProcessControl, so the scene needs one. Tags are names, such as State.Stunned, that an entity carries and that requirements check. Each asset stores a tag made from its Name: Fire Ball gives Ability.FireBall. The entity carries this tag while it has the ability, and keeps the ability's level under it. Each section below matches the inspector section of the same name. The inspector's header shows the ability's one line, as The Forge's Summary column does: each effect it applies, by its first impact across its levels, then its costs and its cooldown, as "-450/-600/-750 Health; 280/420/680 Mana; 70/60/50 s". A number that reads what the editor can't give it, as the target, is marked *. Identity Name: the ability's display name. It also gives the asset tag, so renaming the ability changes its tag. Update anything that names the old tag. Description: free text for your UI. The inspector header shows it. Asset Tag: read-only, made from the Name: punctuation is dropped, and each word is capitalised and joined. The tag is stored when you edit the Name. If the stored tag differs from the one the Name gives, it shows in warning text with an Update button that stores the new one. Textures: icons, each paired with a tag. The texture tagged Primary is the ability's icon. Without one, the first texture is used. Leveling An ability has its own level on each entity that learns it, kept under the ability's asset tag. Effects the ability applies take this level, so their scalers can pick per-level values. A scaler is a value source, such as a table with one value per level. A level provider is an asset whose level range another asset follows. Link Mode: Standalone (default) keeps the ability's own range. Linked To Provider takes the range from a level provider instead. Starting Level (default 1) and Max Level (default 4): the ability's own range. An entity's Starting Abilities begin at the Starting Level, and the ability's level never goes below it. Level Provider, while linked: the asset the range comes from, an Entity, Ability, Effect, Item or Attribute Set. Right-click the field to pick from one type. A link that would make a loop is refused, with an error in the Console. While no provider is set, a warning says the ability uses its own range. While linked, Starting Level and Max Level show the range in use, read-only. Ignore When Level Zero (default on): the ability can't activate while its level is 0. With a Starting Level of 0, the entity must raise the ability's level before it can use it. Link Cost & Cooldown links this ability's cost and cooldown effects to it, so their per-level values follow its range. Unlink Cost & Cooldown removes the links that point at this ability. Each asks first, and one Undo takes it back. Code changes an ability's level through the entity's GAS, with SetLevel or ModifyLevel and the ability's asset tag. An ability that an Item grants starts at the item's level, kept within this range. The link serves the inspector and the tooltips that AbilityInspector builds. At runtime, the ability's level stays within its own Starting Level and Max Level, even while it is linked. Tags Context Tags describe the ability, such as Spell or Melee. The changes made by effects this ability applies carry them as context, and workers can filter by them. They are not applied to the entity. Passive Tags are applied to the entity while it has the ability. Active Tags are applied to the entity while an activation of the ability is running. Activation This section is how the ability starts. One activation goes through these steps: The caster's tag requirements and Caster Checks are checked (see Requirements), and the ability's level (see Leveling). The Targeting task runs, if there is one. If targeting found a target, every check and requirement is checked again, the target's included. It winds up: what its components and its entity's wait for before it starts, as a turn to face its target (see Turn To Face). An interrupt here cancels it, and its cost and cooldown, paid after, aren't. The Asset Loaders run (see Stages). The Stages run, one after another. These steps start inside the call that asks for the ability, AbilitySystemComponent.TryActivateAbility, and run until a task waits. So an ability whose tasks all finish at once has ended, and its callbacks have fired, by the time the call returns. An ability asked for again while that call still runs, from its own callbacks or from another ability's that it started, starts in the next frame instead. When the entity ends, its running abilities end with it, critical or not, and it takes no more activations. Code asks for an ability by its slot, with a request from CreateActivationRequest, by its asset (TryActivateAbility(ability)), or by a tag (TryActivateAbility(tag)). A tag activates the first ability, by slot, whose asset tag or one of whose context tags is that tag or under it. Each form returns an ActivationResult, whose Status says what came of the request: Started, Buffered (it waits in the input buffer), NextFrame (it was asked for while its own activation call still ran, so it starts in the next frame), or Refused. The result reads as true where the request wasn't refused, so if (abilities.TryActivateAbility(ability)) asks whether it was taken. Each form can say why it was refused, through its result's Refusal or an out ActivationRefusal: its Reason, such as Cooldown, Cost, Requirements, Blocked or Busy, and for another caster check, that check's name in Rule; for Crowd Control, Rule is the rule's tag, as Stunned. Where a check or a component refused it, its Detail says why in the check's own words, as "Its caster's Mana, 10, can't pay 50". The ability system's OnAbilityRefused callback tells each refusal as it happens. A request that waits in the input buffer isn't refused, and isn't told again as the buffer retries it. A check on the target comes after targeting and ends the activation instead, nothing of it paid: the request said nothing was refused, as the activation had started, so the callback tells it, as Target, Rule naming the check and Detail saying why. A component that refuses the target its targeting picked, as a Cast Range refuses one beyond it, is told the same way, as the kind its RefusedAs says, Range for a Cast Range, its reason in Rule and Detail. The request's data can carry magnitudes for the effects the ability applies: data.SetByCaller(tag, magnitude), which a Set By Caller scaler on each effect reads (see EFFECTS.md). So a caller that knows the damage as it casts passes it in, and one effect serves every strength. When Busy: what happens when the ability is asked to activate while another ability is busy. An activation is busy, or holds its claim, while its targeting and its critical tasks run. A critical task is one that must not overlap another ability's critical work, such as an attack animation. The inspector marks critical tasks and stages Critical. An ability waits on the claims of abilities that use the same choice, and an ability with critical tasks also waits on any ability with critical tasks that holds its claim, whatever its choice. Entity's Policy (default): use the entity's When Busy, set in the Entity asset's Abilities section. Activate Anyway: start at once. It is refused, as Critical, only when it has critical tasks and another ability with critical tasks holds its claim. Refuse: start only when no Refuse ability holds its claim. Otherwise the request is refused, as Busy. With critical tasks, it is also refused, as Critical, while another ability with critical tasks holds its claim. Queue: when a Queue ability holds its claim, or, for an ability with critical tasks, any ability with critical tasks holds its claim, or a running stage blocks this ability (see Stages), wait in the input buffer for up to Buffer Window seconds of the caster's time, then let go. The buffer holds one request for each ability, and a new press replaces it, with its window afresh. As a claim is released, and each frame, the request with the highest Buffer Priority that can start does, and of equals, the newest. While the entity is paused or its time is stopped, as in a hit-stop, the windows wait too. A request can name a window of its own (CreateActivationRequest's bufferWindow). Whatever the choice, an ability can't start again while its own activation holds its claim. Buffer Window (default 0.3 s) and Buffer Priority (default 0): the input buffer's, under Queue, as above, each a number field read at the ability's level. A window of 0 doesn't wait, so the request is refused. They show under Queue and under the entity's policy, which may be Queue, and are hidden under the others. Activate At Start: when the ability is one of the entity's Starting Abilities, it tries to activate once, as the entity's GAS starts. An ability that an item or code grants later doesn't try it. Triggers: what sets the ability off on its own. A Gameplay Event trigger activates it when code sends the entity an event under the trigger's tag, or a tag under it, with SendGameplayEvent(tag, data), and the ability gets the event's data, its target among it. A Tag Added trigger activates it as the entity gains the tag, or one under it, that it didn't have; more of a tag it holds sets off nothing. Each trigger tries the ability as a request would, so its checks and its When Busy still hold. The core's own events, sent only where an ability listens for them: Impact Dealt, to the dealer, and Impact Taken, to the one hit, as an impact lands between two entities; Kill, to the killer, and Died, to the one who died, its killer the source of the last blow it took; Revived, to a staying entity as it revives; Blocked and Evaded, to one that stops an effect by a Block or Evade stage, and Hit Blocked and Hit Evaded, to its dealer. Their data hold the instigator as Source, the entity it was done to as Subject, and an impact as Impact. For an impact event, a trigger takes only impacts on its Attribute, a Sign (Loss or Gain), and its Impact Types. Its Chance rolls once for each event: Counter Helix's 20%, its Chance Roll pseudo-random or lucky (EFFECTS.md). Its Target is the ability's own targeting, as an area spin finds the enemies round it; the event's Instigator, as a counterattack; or its Subject, as an on-hit ability targets the one hit. An ability set off by Died runs on a dead entity only if its rules don't ask that its caster be alive. The Problems view notes a Gameplay Event trigger on an event neither the core nor an asset in the project sends, as a threshold's Event or a stop stage's does, as only code can send it; and warns of an Impact Dealt or Impact Taken trigger's impact type that no effect deals, which never matches. Chance to Activate: how likely an activation is to start, from 0 to 1, rolled once for each, a player's or a trigger's, after its other checks; a miss is refused with Chance. Activation Roll makes it pseudo-random or lucky, and shows for a chance that can miss. Proc Coefficient: what its effects' hits carry for on-hit effects, where an effect sets none of its own. Ignores Crowd Control: the crowd control rules the ability ignores, by their tags, as Black King Bar's Avatar ignores Silenced: the other rules still stop it, and still interrupt it as it runs (see Requirements). A tag ignores the rules under it too. Cost and Cooldown: gameplay effects (EFFECTS.md) applied to the caster as the ability starts, after its targeting, so a cancelled targeting pays nothing, or by the stage that takes them (see Stages). A cost is usually an Instant effect that lowers a resource such as Mana. A cooldown is usually a Durational effect: while it is active, the caster carries its asset tag, and the Cooldown check refuses the ability. A line under each field says how its effect takes its levels, and Link makes it take this ability's. New, beside an empty field, makes an effect linked to this ability. If Project Settings → PlayForge names a Cost or Cooldown effect, the field's right-click menu copies it or uses it. Attribute Costs, after Cost: what the ability spends of attributes as it's used, beside its Cost effect, both paid. Each names the Attribute it spends, or, where it names none, a Role whose attribute in the project it spends (ATTRIBUTES.md), and an Amount that can scale by level. It's refused with Cost while its caster has less than they come to, lacks the attribute, or no attribute plays the role, and they're paid where a Cost is, as the ability starts or its stage applies usage. The section's line says them, as "30 Mana". Targeting: the task that picks what the ability acts on, such as an entity the player clicks, or the caster itself. Targeting holds the activation's claim. If the task fails while its Break Runtime On Invalid is on, or it doesn't finish, the activation ends. Leave Targeting empty to skip this step. Click targeting (the Select tasks: Position, Direction, GAS Target, GAS Or Position, GAS Target In Range) waits for a press and aims along the game's input, ForgeInput.Current. By default that's the Input System's pointer, a mouse, a pen or a touch, where its package is in and on, or else the Input Manager's mouse, each aimed through Camera.main. With no camera, a press aims nowhere. For a camera of your own, give the default one (new LegacyPointerInput { Camera = camera }, or InputSystemPointerInput), and for a gamepad's reticle or a controller's ray, write an IForgeInput. Put either in with ForgeInput.Use(input). An activation that already holds its target, under TargetReal, or its point, under Position, as an AI's does, takes it with no click, unless the task's Take Target From Data is off; a handed target the task can't take, out of range or failing its requirements, fails the targeting at once. Auto targeting (Auto Target, Auto Target By Affinity) takes the entities within its Range, or its ability's Cast Range where it has one, the range measured from the caster and Use Cast Range on, sorted by its Mode, up to Max Targets, or every one at 0. Each is a target of the activation, and the first, the nearest for Nearest, is its primary. Apply Effects and Apply/Remove Effects reach each target, in the project's resolve order unless their Use Resolve Order is off (EFFECTS.md), so an area ability is Auto Target and then Apply Effects. A Target row and the Target Checks check the primary. Auto Target From Data with Primary Only off takes each target its key holds. Each entity is found by its position, on either hub, with no collider needed. Around says where the range is measured from: the caster, the activation's target (as an AI hands it, or a task before it in a Composite picks it), or its point; Flat, on by default, measures along the ground, and off, a sphere. Use Physics finds entities with physics instead, by collider on its Detection Layers, which show under it alone, as it did, and a runtime entity by its position. Takes says whom each takes by how each stands to its caster: its Enemies, its Allies, itself among them, its Other Allies, Self, All But Self or Everyone; Auto Target takes All But Self to start, and Auto Target By Affinity its Enemies. A targeting task's numbers, as its Range, its Max Targets, a pointer task's Max Distance and an attribute condition's value, are numbers that can scale by level or read an attribute, read as its activation starts, at its ability's level. A pointer's Mouse Button picks one of three, so it stays a choice. Use Implicit Targeting (default off): before targeting, record the caster as the activation's target, under Implicit Tag (default Target), which shows while this is on. A targeting task that sets a target replaces it. The Passive preset turns it on, as a passive gives its holder its effects. Stages This section is what the ability does once it has started. Asset Loaders: run once per activation, after targeting. Each loader adds assets to the activation's data under a tag. A Set Effects loader, for example, adds effects under Effects. Code-driven tasks read them from there. Cancelled By: abilities, by asset tag or a context tag, or a child of one, that cancel this one as they activate. The ability is interrupted, then the other starts. Each stage that names none of its own takes this list, and so does targeting. A critical stage is committed, so nothing cancels it. Blocks: abilities, named the same way, that can't activate while this one runs. Each stage that names none takes this list. A blocked activation is refused, unless When Busy is Queue: then it waits in the input buffer for the block to lift. Stages: each stage starts all its tasks together. The next stage starts when it ends. A stage folds to one line of what it holds, as "2 tasks · All · Applies usage effects", and shows Critical on its row while a task commits the ability to it. The list's − removes the selected stage, and a stage keeps its fold as others are removed or dragged. Completion: All ends the stage when every task has finished. Any ends it when the first task finishes, and cancels the rest. A stage with no policy set behaves as All. Apply Usage Effects: apply the ability's cost and cooldown in this stage. They apply once per activation, in the first stage that does this. If no stage does, they apply as the ability starts, after its targeting. At Stage Start, under Apply Usage Effects: on, apply them as the stage starts. Off, apply them as it ends, and only if it succeeded. Tasks: the work, such as Apply Effects, Delay or Run Sequence, in a list whose + adds an empty task to pick a kind for, from a searchable picker in which each task sits under its category: Effects, Asset Loaders, Process, Sequence, Waits, Events and Tags, Movement, Items and Utility. A task of your own names its submenu with [ForgeMenu("Effects", Description = "...")], a slash nesting one submenu in another and a class's path holding for those made from it; one that names none sits after the submenus, and its Description is what the picker's Context says while it's highlighted. A task's numbers, as Delay's milliseconds and Channel's duration, are numbers that can scale by level, read as it runs, at its ability's level. Run Sequence runs the sequence a static method makes, picked in Sequence by name, from a searchable dropdown of the project's [TaskSequenceMethod] methods, each class's under its name where more than one class holds them, or, for an ability built in code, a fresh run of the sequence its Definition describes, which TaskSequenceBuilder makes. Its Clock picks the clock that sequence runs by: none for the sequence's own or the caster's, or the Caster's, the Game's, Unscaled, which runs while the game is paused, or Scaled, a pace of its own; the ability's other tasks keep the caster's. A stage that holds a critical task is critical. PlayForge's own tasks, by category: Effects, Apply Effects, Apply/Remove Effects, Area Effect (its effects on each within its radius of its caster, its target or its point, its caster where the activation has neither, of those it takes, by position on either hub or with physics) and Apply To Caster; Asset Loaders, the Set tasks; Process, Create Mono Process, Run Process and Disjoint; Sequence, Run Sequence and Inject; Waits, Delay, Channel, and Wait For Event, Wait For Tag (gained or lost) and Wait For Attribute (crossing a value), on its caster or its target, each with a Timeout and a Record As for a later stage's Condition, an event waited for being sent by the core while it waits; Events and Tags, Send Event, to the caster or the targets, Grant Tags, loose tags while its stage runs, and Cancel Abilities, the caster's running ones by tag, but in a critical stage; Movement, Dash and Blink, which tell a mover of the game's own, an IForgeMover on the caster's object, as the Creator Lab's units are; Items, Consume Item, which its item system's Item Consumed hears; Cues, Play Cue, its cues at the stage's moment, on the caster, on the target or at the point; Utility, Unity Event. Dash, Blink, Area Effect, Apply To Caster and Consume Item were the Demo's own. The activation keeps its claim until its last critical stage ends. With no critical stage, it lets the claim go as the stages start. Apply Effects' Record Landed As tags the activation's data as an effect lands on a target, for a later stage's Condition. Condition: when the stage runs, by a tag. With none, always. Otherwise only while the tag is there, or, with When Missing, only while it isn't: Looked For On The Activation looks in the activation's data, as Record Landed As fills it, and Caster or Target in that entity's tags. Both show once the condition names a tag. A stage whose condition fails is skipped. Two stages that name one tag, one wanting it and one wanting it missing, branch: a jab's hit recovery and its whiff. A critical stage that's skipped lets the claim go as the next stage starts, so put a committed whiff before the hit's recovery, and the claim goes as that recovery starts. Cancelled By and Blocks: the stage's own lists, as above, which hold while it runs. A heavy attack's recovery can name the specials that cut it short, and its windup none. Requirements Requirements are what an activation must pass. If one fails, the ability doesn't run. The tag requirements table holds tag checks, a row for each side. Caster checks the caster, with the Caster Checks. While active checks the caster for as long as the ability runs: when it fails, the ability is interrupted, so a channel that must not have State.Stunned ends as a stun lands, and while it fails, the ability can't activate. Target checks the target the same way, after targeting. Each row's Requires cell lists the tags the entity must have, and its Must not have cell the tags it must not have, such as State.Stunned, or says None. A row passes when the entity has every tag it requires and none it must not have, so an empty row always passes. Click a cell to edit its list under the table, with the row's Template and Sync With Template (see EFFECTS.md). Each entry is a tag query: a Tag, a Match mode such as Include Children, and a comparison with a number. Greater Than 0 means "the tag is present". Caster Checks check the caster. They run when the ability is asked to activate, before targeting, and again after targeting. The defaults are Cooldown, Cost and Is Alive. You pick each check's type from a list, which offers the caster's types and those that check either side. Target Checks check the target, after targeting. The default is Is Alive. If targeting found no target, they are skipped. Their list offers the target's types and those that check either side. A check a component stands behind shows under its list, locked, as Check Range does under the Target Checks while the ability holds a Cast Range. No list holds it: it comes and goes with its component, which enforces it, and the section's line counts it among the checks. The check types, by the list that offers them: Caster Checks: Cooldown: passes when the ability isn't cooling down, or, with its charges counted (see Charges), has one in hand. Cost: passes when the ability has no cost, or the cost would leave each attribute it spends at 0 or more, and its Attribute Costs can be paid. The caster must have each attribute. Ability Level: compares the ability's level with Level, using Comparison, as a form it unlocks at a rank. It starts at 2 or more. Either list, checking the caster among the Caster Checks and the target among the Target Checks: Is Alive: passes when the checked entity isn't dead. Attribute: compares the checked entity's Current value of Attribute with Value, using Comparison; with Share Of Base, its share of its base, from 0 to 1, as "below half its health". Tag Weight: compares the checked entity's weight of Tag with Weight, using Comparison, as combo points or stacks. It starts at 1 or more; an entity without the tag holds it at 0. Has Effect: passes when the checked entity has Effect on, or any effect tagged Tagged or under it, by its asset tag, a context tag or a tag it grants; with Without, when it has none of it. Naming neither, it passes. Holds Item: passes when the checked entity holds Item, or, with Equipped, wears it. Naming none, it passes. Condition: passes while its condition, When, holds, as an effect's requirements and an On Hit read theirs: a tag, an attribute, a level, a comparison of numbers, or a condition of your own (see SCALERS.md). It's read against the activation, with the checked entity as its target, so among the Caster Checks its target is the caster. With none, it passes. Target Checks: Affiliation: passes when the target stands to its caster as Target says, as a search's Takes does. Its Enemies share none of the caster's sides and its Allies one, the caster itself among them; Other Allies leaves the caster out, Self is the caster alone, All But Self anyone else, and Everyone anyone. A caster with no sides takes anyone as either. Line of Sight: passes when nothing on the Blocking layers blocks a line from the caster to its target, run Height above each, so the ground under them doesn't. 3D physics colliders block it; triggers and the two ends' own colliders don't. Facing: passes when the target lies within Angle in front of its caster, or, with Behind Target, the caster stands within the angle behind its target, as a backstab wants. Each faces as its targeting packet does, along the ground: 90 takes 45° to either side, and 360 anywhere. Check Range: the Cast Range component's, which no list offers. It shows while the ability holds a Cast Range, saying its range, and passes, as the component enforces the range (see Cast Range). A failed Caster Check refuses the activation as the kind its RefusedAs says: Cooldown, Cost or Dead for those three, which name none, and Rule, naming the check, for any other; a failed Target Check ends it after targeting, told as Target, naming the check (see Activation). Each says why in Validate's error, which the refusal carries as its Detail, as "Its caster's Mana, 20, can't pay 30". A check of your own implements IAbilityValidationRule: Validate says whether the activation passes, and why not, and GetName names it; RefusedAs, Rule unless it says otherwise, is the kind its refusal of the caster is told as, so an ammunition check can say Cooldown as the built-in does. [ForgeMenu] names and describes it in the list, and [ValidationSide] says which list offers it, Caster or Target; without it, both do. A component stands behind a check by overriding its TargetCheck or CasterCheck with an AbstractComponentValidationRule<T> of its own kind: the check shows under the list while the ability holds the component, and the component enforces it, in CanStart. The section's Clear button empties the tag requirements and leaves the checks, since an ability without them would skip its cost and cooldown. Crowd Control Crowd control holds for every ability at once, so no ability has to list Stunned among the tags it must not have. A Crowd Control Rules asset (Create → PlayForge → Crowd Control Rules) holds its rules, each a Tag the caster carries, as Stunned, and what it Stops: Every Ability, as a stun, or Abilities Tagged, those whose asset tag or a context tag is one of its Ability Tags or under it, as Silenced stops spells and Disarmed attacks. An entity's abilities follow its own Crowd Control (ENTITIES.md), or, where it names none, its Forge Project's (ATTRIBUTES.md). While the caster carries a rule's tag, or one under it, an ability the rule stops is refused with Crowd Control, the refusal's Rule naming the tag, and one that runs is interrupted as the tag lands, as a stun breaks a channel. An ability's Ignores Crowd Control (see Activation) opts it out of the rules it names. Code asks with rules.Stopping(ability, tags), the first rule that stops the ability, or null. Components An ability's components are features it carries, each a class with hooks into its life, added with the list's +. A component hears the ability Granted to an entity and Removed from it; is asked whether an activation may start, CanStart, where a reason it gives refuses the activation, named by it, as the kind its RefusedAs says, Rule unless it says otherwise; is asked whether the target its targeting picked may be taken, CanTakeTarget, where a reason it gives ends the activation there, before anything of it is paid, told as the kind its RefusedAs says; is waited on as an activation winds up, WindUp, after its target checks and before its cost, as a turn to face its target is; and hears an activation Start, Commit its cost and cooldown, and End, by how it ended: done, cancelled or failed. As the activation's usage applies, a component may apply it in the ability's place, ApplyUsage, as a Toggle does, composing its own from the spec's PayCosts and SpendCooldown; may waive the Cost and Cooldown checks while it says so, Waives; and claims the categories of the effects its ability puts on for a purge, CategoryOf, as a Toggle claims its effect a toggle's. A kind that makes no sense twice is offered only while the ability holds none of it. A component of your own derives from AbstractAbilityComponent and overrides the hooks it needs, each a no-op otherwise. It's the ability's, shared by everything that holds it, so what it keeps for one entity's ability it keeps through its context: ctx.GetState<T>(this). Describe says what it does in one line with its numbers, as a Cast Range's "Range 600", which the Components section's line, The Forge's summary and the ability's breakdown say beside its name; and DescribeUsage what it adds to the ability's use, as Charges' "3 charges", which the Activation section's line says after its cost and cooldown. Its rules in the editor derive from ForgeComponentRule<T>, in the editor's assembly, with a public constructor that takes nothing: the Problems view runs each on every asset that holds a component of its kind, and the ability's inspector says what it finds under its Components list, as it says the Charges'. Code finds a component by what it does, not by its class: Find<T>(), on an ability, its spec, an effect, an item and an entity, gives the first of its components that is a T, a kind or an interface it implements. An ability's reach is an IAbilityReach, which Cast Range implements; the targeting tasks, the Creator Lab's bots and your own code read it through ForgeReach, so a component of your own that implements it is asked as a Cast Range is. How its uses come back is an ICooldownModel, which Charges implements: how many it holds, how many are in hand, what a use spends, and why the Cooldown check refuses it with none; an ability with none has SingleCooldown, one use, back as its Cooldown ends. The Cooldown check asks it, the ability spends through it, and a HUD reads it as spec.CooldownModel. A component's state that needs its holder, as a Charges component's charges need their ability, is kept with spec.ComponentStates.TryGet and Keep. The built-in components are written on this API alone, and PlayForge's core names none of them, so a component of your own reaches as far as they do. None has a shortcut: code reads one through Find<T>() or the component itself, as spec.Find<ToggleAbilityComponent>()?.IsOn(spec) says whether a Toggle is on. Cast Range A Cast Range component is the one range the ability has: how far from its caster its target or its point may be, its Range a number that can scale by level, measured along the ground unless Flat is off; 0 reaches anywhere. An activation handed a target or a point beyond it, under TargetReal or Position, as an AI's is, is refused as Range, so nothing of it is paid and an AI can walk closer and ask again; targeting that picks a target beyond it, whichever task picked it, ends the activation before its stages, told as Range too. The auto-targeting tasks measured from the caster, and Select GAS Target In Range, search within it where their Use Cast Range is on, as it is by default, their own range set aside. The Creator Lab's units attack from their attack's Cast Range, and its bots cast an ability once their foe is within its Cast Range, where it has one (CREATOR_LAB.md). It's the ability's reach, an IAbilityReach: code reads it through ForgeReach, as ForgeReach.TryRead(caster, ability, out range), and a reach of your own takes its place in each of these. While the ability holds it, its Target Checks show its Check Range, locked, saying the range (see Requirements). An ability holds one at most. Charges A Charges component says how many uses the ability holds, a number that can scale by level, each use spending a charge. With 1 it is an ordinary cooldown. With more, the Cooldown check refuses it only with none in hand, and its Recharge says how spent ones come back: Each Charge (the default) starts the Cooldown for each charge spent, a container of its own whatever the effect does when applied again, and each brings its charge back as it ends, so three spent a second apart come back a second apart; All At Once starts the Cooldown only as the last is spent, and its end brings them all back. Write a recharge of your own by extending AbstractChargeRecharge: override InHand (how many are in hand) and Spend (what a use does), using AbilityCharges' Max, Spent, Cooldowns and StartCooldown; one of your own counts even a single charge, unless its CountsASingleCharge says not. Charges are the ability's cooldown model (see Components), so code reads what's in hand of any ability as spec.CooldownModel.InHand(spec). The component itself, spec.Find<ChargesAbilityComponent>(), holds its Charges and Recharge, and its ChargesOf(spec) gives the ability's charges on its caster, an AbilityCharges. The section's line counts them, as "3 charges", and a warning under the Components list, as in the Problems view, says where built-in charges have no Cooldown to bring them back, so they never run out. An ability holds one at most. Toggle A Toggle component holds an Effect the ability turns on and off on its caster, as a mana shield: used, it puts the effect on where its usage would be paid, paying its Cost and Attribute Costs and starting no cooldown; used again, it takes the effect off, paying nothing and asking no cost, and starts its Cooldown, or spends a charge. Neither its cost nor its cooldown stops it turning off. It counts only the effect it put on; one another put there leaves it off. A purge counts its effect a Toggle's, as a death that keeps toggles keeps it. Code asks the component, spec.Find<ToggleAbilityComponent>(): its IsOn(spec) says whether its effect is on, and its Effect is the effect. It's written on the components' hooks alone: it applies the usage in its ability's place, waives the cost and the cooldown while it's on, and claims its effect. The Problems view warns where it toggles an Instant effect, which is never on. As its holder forgets the ability, the effect comes off; it stayed on. An ability holds one at most. Turn To Face A Turn To Face component says how this ability turns its caster to face its target or its point before its first stage, in place of its entity's Turns To Face (ENTITIES.md): its own Turn Speed, Start Angle, Facing Angle, If Too Long and Max Wait. With Turns off it doesn't turn at all, as a cast behind its caster doesn't. The Target Checks come before the turn, so a Facing check that wants its target in front of its caster reads the caster's facing before it turns. An ability holds one at most. Auras An Aura component holds an effect on those near its holder, while the entity knows the ability, as a banner that inspires the allies round its bearer: each a radius, whom it takes, its holder too or not, and how often it checks (EFFECTS.md). Cues A Cues component plays what the ability shows and sounds at its moments, on its caster: On Activate as an activation starts, On Commit as it pays its cost and starts its cooldown, While Active from its start to its end, On End as it ends however it ended, and On Refused as one is refused, nothing of it paid. Each list holds cues as an effect's does (EFFECTS.md), a Cue Tag among them; a Prefab cue in While Active lasts until the activation ends. A stage's exact moment, as a sword's arc, plays through a Play Cue task. An ability holds one at most. Workers Workers are reusable behaviours, picked from a list, that react to what happens to an entity. This group is subscribed to the entity when it learns the ability, and removed when the ability is removed. Name labels the group. It holds four lists: Attribute workers run before or after an attribute changes, for example to reduce incoming damage. Impact workers inspect the changes this entity deals. Tag workers react when the entity's tags change. Analysis workers examine the frame at its end, for example to detect death. Each list's + adds an empty worker to pick a kind for. The section's import button copies a worker group from another asset. On Hit On Hit, above the workers, holds the effects the entity's hits apply while it knows the ability, as a passive's. Its entries are an item's: an attribute, the effects, to the one hit or the holder, only on a kill, impact types and a condition (ITEMS.md). Modifiers Modifiers, under On Hit, change other effects as they're made, while the entity knows the ability: its holder's own, as a boon that adds a burst to its holder's every Chill, or those landing on it, as a cloak that halves the stuns its wearer takes. Each entry is a rule of its own or names a shared Effect Modifier asset (EFFECTS.md). Lifesteal An ability gives its holder lifesteal by an effect that raises the holder's Lifesteal, the attribute the project's Lifesteal worker names as its Share, as a passive applies it to its caster, which the Lifesteal worker heals by (WORKERS.md): a vampiric mask's Infinite effect of +0.15 Lifesteal heals its wearer 15% of each blow it deals. Its Lifesteal list is gone. Local Data Local Data is a list of named values stored on the asset. Each row has a Key (a tag) and a value of a kind: Float, Int, String, Bool, Tag, Attribute, Effect, Ability, Entity, Object, MonoBehaviour or ScriptableObject, or a kind of your own, a [Serializable] class made from LocalDataValue<T>, as a point or a colour, which the row's kinds offer beside PlayForge's. A row saves its own value alone. Object fields take project assets, not scene objects. Code reads a value by its type, data.TryGet(out float range) or data.TryGet(out MyPoint point), and a number, a Float or an Int, which can scale, with data.Value.TryReadNumber(context, out float number). Code reads a value with ability.TryGetLocalData(key, out var data). The first row with that key wins. A tag check of your own, extending AbstractTagValidationRule, reads its tag's value with GetValue: the tag's weight on the entity it checks or, where that entity holds none of it, the ability's Local Data under the tag. Used By The PlayForge assets that refer to this ability, each with its type icon, such as an entity that starts with it, an item that grants it, or a cost linked to it. Click a row to select the asset. The list follows the project as it changes.

guides/ATTRIBUTES.html.title: PlayForge — Attributes | PlayForge
guides/ATTRIBUTES.html.summary: PlayForge — Attributes An Attribute asset names one number an entity can have, such as Health, Mana or Strength. An entity is anything that runs a gameplay ability system (GAS), such as the player or an enemy. The asset holds no value. An entity gets its starting values for the attribute from its Attribute Set, and gameplay effects change them from there. At runtime each entity holds two values for each of its attributes. Base is the value the attribute is measured against, and Current is the value in play. For a pool such as Health, Base is the maximum and Current is what is left. For a stat such as Strength, the two are often the same. The Attribute Set's bounds keep them in range (see ATTRIBUTE_SETS.md). Attribute sets, effects, validation rules and workers refer to the attribute asset itself. An attribute has no asset tag. Each section below matches the inspector section of the same name. A collapsed section shows one line about what it holds, such as the abbreviation or how many assets use the attribute. Identity Name: the attribute's display name. Give each attribute its own Name: some lookups compare attributes by Name, such as an attribute worker matching the attribute it watches. Abbreviation: a short form, such as HP. The collapsed section shows it. Description: free text for your UI. Textures: icons, each paired with a tag. The texture tagged Primary is the attribute's icon. Without one, the first texture is used. Role: what the attribute is, which says how bonuses to it add up and how a number reads it: Value, every attribute's unless it says: bonuses add and multiply as each effect says, and a number reads it as it is. Bonus Share, as Damage Amplification at 0.2 for 20%: bonuses add, +20% and +30% making 0.5, and × Attribute reads it as a multiplier, 1 + x, so an attack of 100 that reads it deals 150. Multiplier, as Damage Dealt at 1: as a Value, read as it is. Resistance, a share taken off or a chance, as Damage Resistance: bonuses stack with diminishing returns, each on what's left, so two of 30% make 51% and none takes it past 1; × Attribute reads what's left, 1 − x. The lasting bonuses diminish; a permanent change, which an instant or periodic impact commits, adds as it is. Barrier, as a shield before Health: it absorbs for the attribute its Absorbs For names, each workable loss to that one coming off it first, as much as it holds, and the rest going on; two hits in a frame soak no more than it holds, and what it soaks comes off it at the frame's end. Decay Per Second, a number field read at its holder's level, takes it down by its holder's own time, a number a second or, with Decay As Share Of Base, that share of its base, as Topaz Brooch's barrier fades; Fades With Effect fades what a lasting effect gives it to 0 by the time that effect ends. A hit the barrier soaks whole is no loss to the other, so an On Hit counting it doesn't go off. Gains Scaled By names an attribute that multiplies each workable gain to this one's current, on the same entity: Health's by Healing Received, so a curse at 0.5 halves heals and Ice Blast's 0 blocks them. A loss passes it by, and a gain to the base, as more maximum, does too. An effect's impact can add its own way (Add Behaviour: as the attribute's role says, a plain Sum, or Diminishing), and a number can read its own way (× Attribute's Read As). An attribute that plays one of its project's roles says so, as "Plays Health in Arena". Roles A game's settings live on its Forge Project, the asset at the root of its folder that The Forge's projects are. Among them are its Roles: the part each attribute plays in the game, each a role tag and the attribute that plays it. PlayForge's own features read the roles it ships, and a game's code reads its own by their tags, so no attribute's name is built in: Health (Tags.ROLE_HEALTH): what an entity dies of as it reaches 0, where no death watcher of its own watches for its death and its Death doesn't say otherwise (ENTITIES.md); what On Hit counts, lifesteal heals and Execute reads where they name no attribute; and whose loss names the killer, for Kill and Died. An entity whose set has no attribute in this role doesn't die of it. Luck (Tags.ROLE_LUCK): read on the caster of every chance that gives no luck of its own. Movement Speed (Tags.ROLE_MOVEMENT_SPEED): what the Creator Lab's units walk at, where its rules name none. A role of your own: any tag, as Role.Energy, in the same list. Code reads it with ForgeRoles.AttributeFor(tag), and an ability's attribute cost can spend it (ABILITIES.md). Each role is optional, and an empty one leaves things as they were. Project Settings → PlayForge shows the active project's settings under Forge Project: Fill Roles by Name fills each of PlayForge's roles no attribute plays yet with the project's attribute of its name, and Create Forge Project makes the default project where there's none. The settings also hold the project's default Crowd Control (ABILITIES.md). A running game reads its settings from ForgeProject.Current: the project code sets with ForgeProject.Use(project), as a test or a game with no GameRoot does, or else the one its GameRoot names in its Project field. A build has the project because the GameRoot names it, and play mode reads it as a build does, not The Forge's active project. In the editor, the inspectors and the Problems window read each asset against its own project, the one whose folder holds it. The Problems window warns of an attribute cost that spends nothing, or a role no attribute plays in its project; an entity whose starting abilities spend attributes its set doesn't give; and an entity that stays when it dies whose set lacks the Health role's attribute, with no death watcher of its own. Local Data Local Data is a list of named values stored on the asset. Each row has a Key (a tag) and a value of a kind: Float, Int, String, Bool, Tag, Attribute, Effect, Ability, Entity, Object, MonoBehaviour or ScriptableObject, or a kind of your own, a [Serializable] class made from LocalDataValue<T>, as a point or a colour, which the row's kinds offer beside PlayForge's. A row saves its own value alone. Object fields take project assets, not scene objects. Code reads a value by its type, data.TryGet(out float range) or data.TryGet(out MyPoint point), and a number, a Float or an Int, which can scale, with data.Value.TryReadNumber(context, out float number). PlayForge doesn't read an attribute's Local Data itself. Your code and workers can, with attribute.TryGetLocalData(key, out var data). The first row with that key wins. Used By The PlayForge assets that refer to this attribute, each with its type icon: the Attribute Sets that give its starting values, the Gameplay Effects that change it, and the validation rules and ability costs that check or spend it. Click a row to select the asset. The list follows the project as it changes.

guides/ATTRIBUTE_SETS.html.title: PlayForge — Attribute Sets | PlayForge
guides/ATTRIBUTE_SETS.html.summary: PlayForge — Attribute Sets An Attribute Set asset lists the attributes an entity starts with, and how each one starts: its Current and Base values, its bounds and its rounding. An entity is anything that runs a gameplay ability system (GAS), such as the player or an enemy. Its Entity asset names one set. When the GAS initializes, it builds every attribute in the set and in its sub-sets. Each element becomes its attribute's root value, the value before any effect. Gameplay effects then change the attribute on top of that root. A root can follow the entity's level or another attribute, through a cached scaler. It is worked out again whenever the attribute is recalculated. Tags are names, such as State.Stunned, that an entity carries and that requirements check. Each asset stores a tag made from its Name: Hero Stats gives AttributeSet.HeroStats. The entity carries the set's tag and the tags of its sub-sets. Each section below matches the inspector section of the same name. A collapsed section shows one line about what it holds, such as the level range or how many attributes the set gives. Identity Name: the set's display name. It also gives the asset tag, so renaming the set changes its tag. Update anything that names the old tag. Description: free text for your UI. Asset Tag: read-only, made from the Name: punctuation is dropped, and each word is capitalised and joined. The tag is stored when you edit the Name, and the inspector header shows it after the set's type. If the stored tag differs from the one the Name gives, it shows in warning text with an Update button that stores the new one. Textures: icons, each paired with a tag. The texture tagged Primary is the set's icon. Without one, the first texture is used. Leveling The set's level range is the one the cached scalers on its elements are authored for. A cached scaler is a value source for an element, such as a table with one value per level. At runtime those scalers follow the level of the entity that owns the set. Linking the set to that Entity asset gives the scalers one value per entity level. A level provider is an asset whose level range another asset follows. Link Mode: Standalone (default) keeps the set's own range. Linked To Provider takes the range from a level provider instead. Starting Level (default 1) and Max Level (default 4): the set's own range. Cached scalers on its elements whose Level Configuration is Lock To Level Provider use the Max Level to size their per-level values. Level Provider, while linked: the asset the range comes from, an Entity, Ability, Effect, Item or Attribute Set. Right-click the field to pick from one type. A link that would make a loop is refused, with an error in the Console. While no provider is set, a warning says the set uses its own range. While linked, Starting Level and Max Level show the range in use, read-only. Attributes Each element sets up one attribute. Folded, an element shows one line: what its attribute starts at, and its range. Preview In, above the list while another set holds this one as a sub-set: This Set, or a set that holds it, directly or through another. An entity built from that set starts with these attributes as part of it, so the elements and All Attributes show their values there, with that set's collisions and the attributes it gives. The choice lasts until the editor closes. Attribute (in the element's row): the attribute asset. Starts At: what the attribute starts at, at each of the set's levels, as "100/120/140/160", with the levels on the right; Current and Base apart, as "Current 50 · Base 80", when they differ; or a range past six levels. It is worked out as the runtime works it out: an entity at each level, built from the set, with its sub-sets, collisions, scalers, bounds and rounding, before any effect, item or worker acts on it. A note says when another element's value is the one used, and a warning says when a scaler reads an attribute the set doesn't give, which reads 0. Base and Current: each a magnitude field, as an effect's are: a number, or a cached scaler with how the number combines with it. One kind of scaler follows the entity's level. Another follows a different attribute, and this attribute is then worked out again whenever that one changes. Each field's menu copies the other side's number and scaler into it. Link Current to Base: Current takes Base's number and scaler, and its own field hides. Bounds: the range the values are held in, with the Floor and Ceiling the policy reads, each a Current and a Base. Zero To Base: Current stays between 0 and Base. Floor To Base: Current stays between the Floor's Current and Base. Base stays at or above the Floor's Base. Zero To Ceil: Current stays between 0 and the Ceiling's Current. Base stays between 0 and the Ceiling's Base. Floor To Ceil: Current and Base each stay between their Floor and Ceiling. Unlimited: no bounds. Right-click a Floor or a Ceiling for No Floor or No Ceiling. A magnitude you type is kept within the bounds. A stored magnitude outside them, as after the bounds change, shows a warning, and the runtime clamps it. Auto Clamp: apply the Bounds. With it off, the Bounds are ignored at runtime. Scale With Base: when Base changes, change Current by the same share. A value of 80/100 that loses half its Base ends at 40/50. Rounding: None, To Floor, To Ceil, Round, or Snap To with a Snap Interval, a number field read at its owner's level. Rounding applies after the Bounds, each time the value changes, so it can make a change bigger or smaller than its effect asked for. Retention Group: the group the root value counts toward. Groups split an attribute's value for queries and UI, such as base and bonus health. They never change the math. Collision: what to do when this attribute appears more than once across the set and its sub-sets. See Collision Settings. Sub-Sets Other attribute sets this set includes. The entity gets their attributes as well, and those of their own sub-sets in turn. Their asset tags are applied to the entity, and their workers are subscribed with this set's. When an attribute appears more than once, Collision Settings decide which value it starts with. Only the Collision Settings of the set the entity names are used. Don't let a set include itself, directly or through another set: nothing stops the loop. All Attributes lists each attribute the set gives, sub-sets included. Collision Settings These settings decide an attribute's root value when it appears in more than one element, across this set and its sub-sets. Elements are taken in order: this set's elements first, then each sub-set's in turn. First, each element's Collision choice puts it in a group. One group decides, picked in this order: Use Set Collision Setting, Use This, Combine, Use Existing. Elements in the other groups are ignored. In the Combine group, the values are added up. Bounds, rounding and the retention group come from the first element. The other groups choose by the Resolution Policy here: Use Maximum (default): the element with the highest Base magnitude. Use Minimum: the element with the lowest Base magnitude. Use Average: the average of the elements' values. Bounds and rounding come from the first element. Use First and Use Last: the first or the last element. Ignore: the first element stands. All Attributes A table of each attribute the set gives an entity, its sub-sets' included, once each: the value its Current starts at, at each level, and the range the set keeps it in. The values are the ones the elements show, in the set this set is previewed in. Hover over a value for its Current and Base at each level, and, where several elements give an attribute, whose value is used. The Entity inspector shows the same table under the entity's Attribute Set, at the entity's levels. Workers Workers are reusable behaviours, picked from a list, that react to what happens to an entity. This group is subscribed when the entity's GAS initializes, with each sub-set's group, and stays for the entity's lifetime. Name labels the group. It holds four lists: Attribute workers run before or after an attribute changes, for example to reduce incoming damage. Impact workers inspect the changes the entity deals. Tag workers react when the entity's tags change. Analysis workers examine the frame at its end, for example to detect death. Each list's + adds an empty worker to pick a kind for. The section's import button copies a worker group from another asset. Local Data Local Data is a list of named values stored on the asset. Each row has a Key (a tag) and a value of a kind: Float, Int, String, Bool, Tag, Attribute, Effect, Ability, Entity, Object, MonoBehaviour or ScriptableObject, or a kind of your own, a [Serializable] class made from LocalDataValue<T>, as a point or a colour, which the row's kinds offer beside PlayForge's. A row saves its own value alone. Object fields take project assets, not scene objects. Code reads a value by its type, data.TryGet(out float range) or data.TryGet(out MyPoint point), and a number, a Float or an Int, which can scale, with data.Value.TryReadNumber(context, out float number). PlayForge doesn't read an attribute set's Local Data itself. Your code and workers can, with set.TryGetLocalData(key, out var data). The first row with that key wins. Used By The PlayForge assets that refer to this set, each with its type icon, such as an entity built from it or a set that holds it as a sub-set. Click a row to select the asset. The list follows the project as it changes.

guides/CREATOR_LAB.html.title: PlayForge — The Creator Lab | PlayForge
guides/CREATOR_LAB.html.summary: PlayForge — The Creator Lab A space for trying a project's own assets: put units down, give them abilities, effects and items, cast, and watch the numbers move. Open it from Window → PlayForge → Creator Lab: it opens in a new scene and plays. The scenes open before are saved first, if you want them saved. The lab plays every PlayForge asset in the project's own folders. The space The ground is a plane in the middle of the scene, lit from above. The camera looks down at an angle. Scroll to pull it back or bring it in; drag with the middle button to pan. The right panel's sliders set its distance and tilt, and Reset view puts it back. Units are a body and a GameplayAbilitySystem: a capsule with a nose to show where it faces, a ring at its feet in its side's color, and a bar over it with its name and health. A unit walks in a straight line where it's sent and attacks what it's set on, and a walk or a stop ends a turn to face its abilities ordered, as a game's move would. PlayForge has no movement of its own, so the lab's is its own: a project's game moves its units its own way. The lab's caster is a unit of the lab's own, on no side, with no body. It's the source of what you drop while no unit is selected. The panels Each panel collapses to a tab at its edge with its − button. Library (left): the active Forge Project's assets by kind, abilities, effects, items, entities, attribute sets, attributes and scalers, each kind by name, or every asset of the project while it has no Forge Project. Project switches the active project, as The Forge does, and follows The Forge's switch. The search box filters them; Refresh lists them again after you make or delete one. A kind's color shows in its icon alone. Selected (middle): hidden until something is selected. Click an asset in the library to see its numbers level by level, as "−80/−120/−160 Health"; Open in The Forge opens it there. Click a unit to see its attributes, tags, effects with their stacks and time left, abilities with their levels and cooldowns, and items. There, − and + change an ability's level, × takes an ability or an item, and Remove takes the unit out. Lab (right): the mode, the test dummies, the camera and the lab's time. Log (bottom): collapsed until you open it, a page for each way the lab shows its working; see below. Dropping assets Drag an asset from the library and drop it on the space: Dropped On What happens An effect A unit It lands on the unit, from the selected unit, or from the lab's caster An ability A unit, or the ground The selected unit, or the lab's caster, casts it there, its target in the activation's data, as click targeting takes it with no click. A unit that doesn't know it learns it first. An ability that needs more than the point waits for a click, which Esc cancels An item A unit It's given to the unit, equipped An entity or an attribute set The ground A test dummy of it is put down, on the side the Lab panel's picker names Test dummies The Test dummies section puts down a dummy of any entity or attribute set, on a side: Blue, Red, Green, Gold or Neutral. A dummy counts what it takes: its damage a second, the last blow by its impact types and the effect it came from, and a short history, which the Selected panel shows. It doesn't die unless asked: falling, it's revived where it stands, at full. Left alone for three seconds, it mends to full. Reset puts each dummy back where it was put, at full; Clear takes every unit out. An effect or an entity changed in the inspector or The Forge as the lab plays is read on its next application, as every asset is. What a unit was made from, its attribute set and its starting abilities, shows on a new unit. Battle The Battle mode fights teams of bots. Pick an entity and a side above, a level in Level, and Add bot; each side stands in a line of its own, Blue to the south, Red to the north, Green to the west and Gold to the east. Quick battle makes Blue against Red, A side of each, of the entity selected in the library, or picked at random from the project's. Play starts the fight and the lab's time; the line under the buttons says who stands, and who won, or that no one stands. Reset makes every bot anew where it started, at full, with the items and abilities you gave it since and their levels. A bot takes the nearest foe it can target, casts what's ready, and otherwise attacks with its attack. Its order and its moments are its rules': Cast Order Key: the Local Data key an entity's order is under, as "W Q E", the letters its abilities other than its attack, in its entity's order. With none, each in turn. Cast When Key: the key for when it casts an ability: InRange (the default), Hurt (below 60% health), Low (below 35%, away from its foe, as an escape), Stunned (while something stops it) or FoeLow (its foe below half). Reach Key: the key for an ability's reach, 0 for anywhere, where it has no reach of its own, as a Cast Range; one that has reaches as far as that does. Low on health, a bot backs off a moment once in a while. The Demo's AI hero is a bot, its roster giving the keys. Your unit In either mode you can play a unit of your own. Put down in the Lab panel's Your unit section puts one of the entity picked above down on the side picked, where the camera looks, and gives you control of it; Take control takes the unit selected, and a bot taken over stops fighting until you let it go, a new fight passing it over and Reset keeping you on its seat's new bot. Release lets it go, and Follow has the camera follow it. The line under the buttons says whom you control. The controls are the Demo's: right-click the ground to walk there, a foe to attack it, or an ally to walk to it; Q, W, E and R cast its abilities past its attack, in its entity's order, and 1 to 6 its items' active abilities; an ability that needs a target waits for a left-click, and Esc cancels it; S stops it. They read PlayForge's input, ForgeInput, so a game's own input or a test's stands in. Its orders go through a driver. The lab's walks a unit in a straight line and casts as the lab's units do. A project whose units move and cast their own way makes a Lab Driver asset (Create → PlayForge → Lab Driver) of its own class, overriding the orders its game gives its own way (MoveTo, Attack, Cast, Stop, each doing as the lab's does unless overridden), and names it on its Lab Rules' Driver. Time The lab's units live in a world of the lab's own (ProcessWorld), which the lab steps by its own time, so its time stands still or runs faster without touching Unity's. Pause stops it, Step goes one frame (a sixtieth of a second) while it's paused, and Speed runs it from a quarter to four times as fast. The camera and the panels go on while it's paused. Showing its working The bottom panel's pages show what happens as the lab plays. Each records only while the lab runs. Journal: the lab's effect journal over every unit: each effect landing, with its number traced, refused and why, ticking, hitting, coming off, and each worker that ran, by its hook and its side, with the actions it queued and whether they ran; newest first, on the selected unit or, with Selected unit off, on any. Click an entry to see its parts: a number's, a hit's breakdown, or a worker's actions. Combat: the selected unit's combat log, newest first, each hit with its steps under it, "-30 as made → Math -30 → -15 (inline) → landed -15". The project's combat log writes it (Project Settings → PlayForge → Combat Log). Stops: a list of what pauses the lab's world: an effect lands, is refused or has a worker run, an attribute crosses a value, a tag comes or goes, an ability is refused, each on the selected unit or any, and naming an effect, an ability, a tag or an attribute where it asks for one (Any for an effect or an ability takes any). As one fires, the world pauses and the page says which and what fired it. Go plays on, Step Frame goes one frame, and Step Tick goes on until an effect ticks on the selected unit, or on any, up to ten seconds, or a stop fires. Watches: pin a number on the selected unit, an attribute's current or base value, a tag's count, an effect's stacks or time left, or a Scaler asset read on it, and see each as a line over the last minute of the lab's time, in its own color and scaled to its own range, with its value now. Log: PlayForge's messages as ForgeLog lets them through, by system, newest first, those about the selected unit where Selected unit is on. System and Level give a system a level of its own, which the Console keeps too; As all gives it back to the Logging preference's. The lab's rules The lab needs to know a few things about a project: which attribute is a unit's health, which it walks at, which tags stop, hide or shield it, and which ability is its attack. With no rules given, it takes the attributes playing the project's Health and Movement Speed roles (ATTRIBUTES.md), or else finds the attributes named Health and Movement Speed (or Move Speed), and walks a unit without a speed at 4 a second. To say more, make a Lab Rules asset (Create → PlayForge → Lab Rules) and give it to the lab's CreatorLab component: Health and Movement Speed, or Walk Speed where a unit has none. Left empty, each is the project's. Stops: tags that stop a unit moving, as Stunned. Hides: tags under which the other side can't see or target it, as Invisible. Shields: tags under which no one can target it. Attack Range Key: the Local Data key a unit's attack range is under, or Attack Range for every unit; a unit whose attack has a reach of its own, as a Cast Range, attacks from as far as it reaches. Attack Slot: which of an entity's starting abilities is its attack, from 0, or −1 for none. Driver: the project's Lab Driver, which the unit you control is ordered about through (Your unit). The Demo's roster is the Demo's rules: its units, camera and dummy are the lab's, so the two can't drift. In code CreatorLab.Create(library, rules, panels) makes a lab, as the tests do. Its calls are the panels': AddUnit and AddDummy, ApplyEffect, CastAt, GiveItem, Drop (at a point of the screen) and DropAt (on a unit or a point), Select, SetMode, ResetDummies, Clear, and Step, Paused, Speed and StepFrame for its time. A library is an ILabLibrary: in the editor every asset of the project (EditorLabLibrary), in code a ListLibrary of the assets given; a game's own build gets ListLibrary.Of(project), the assets its Forge Project's catalog names, which the lab plays where no editor gives it a library. A library offers projects to switch between through ILabLibrary.Projects, Project and UseProject, which have defaults. The unit you control is ControlledUnit, given by PutDownOwnUnit, TakeControl and ReleaseControl, its camera by Follow; the lab's controls are its Controls, a LabControls, whose Driver comes before its rules'. A game's own player can be a LabControls too, as the Demo's is: its unit set on it, or its ControlledUnit() overridden. What it shows of its working is its Showing, a LabShowing: its Journal, an EffectJournal over every unit; its Stops, added with Add(stop), and StoppedBy and StoppedFor as one fires, Resume() to let it go and StepTick(); its Watches, pinned with Pin(watch); and its Log of ForgeLog's messages. A build can leave the lab out by defining PLAYFORGE_NO_LAB. The Demo uses the lab's units, so it goes too.
