guides/ITEMS.html.summary: PlayForge — Items An Item asset describes something an entity can hold and equip, such as a sword or a ring. An entity is anything that runs a gameplay ability system (GAS), such as the player or an enemy. Giving an item puts it in the entity's inventory. Equipping it applies what it grants: its Granted Effects, its Active Ability, its Granted Tags and its workers. Unequipping the item, or removing it from the inventory, takes them away again. An entity gets items from its Entity asset's Starting Items, or from code through its ItemSystemComponent, with GiveItem, EquipItem, UnequipItem and RemoveItem. The entity's limits on items are set on its Entity asset. Tags are names, such as State.Stunned, that an entity carries and that requirements check. Each asset stores a tag made from its Name: Iron Sword gives Item.IronSword. The entity carries this tag while the item is in its inventory, equipped or not, and keeps the item's level under it. Each section below matches the inspector section of the same name. A collapsed section shows one line about what it holds, such as the level range or how many effects the item grants. The inspector's header shows the item's one line, as The Forge's Summary column does: what each effect it gives changes while it's equipped, by its first impact across its levels, then the ability it grants, as "+20 Armor; Blink". Identity Name: the item's display name. It also gives the asset tag, so renaming the item changes its tag. Update anything that names the old tag. Description: free text for your UI. Asset Tag: read-only, made from the Name: punctuation is dropped, and each word is capitalised and joined. The tag is stored when you edit the Name, and the inspector header shows it after the item's type. If the stored tag differs from the one the Name gives, it shows in warning text with an Update button that stores the new one. Visibility: a tag your UI can read for filtering, such as Always Visible or Not Visible. The Forge lists it. The runtime doesn't act on it. Textures: icons, each paired with a tag. The texture tagged Primary is the item's icon. Without one, the first texture is used. Max Stack Size: how many of the item one inventory slot holds, a number field read at the item's level, as StackSizeOf(spec) reads it. 1 or less, and each is a slot of its own. Whether an inventory may hold an item more than once is the entity's choice, through its Allow Duplicate Items setting (see ENTITIES.md). Stacking A give fills the item's stack first, up to its Max Stack Size, and takes no new slot. A full stack opens another only with Allow Duplicate Items on; without it, what doesn't fit isn't taken. ItemSystemComponent.GiveItem(item, count) takes what fits and returns how many it took, and GiveItem(item, out index) gives one, into the stack if there's room. RemoveItem(item, count) takes stacks off, from the last slot first, and a slot whose last stack comes off goes; RemoveItem(item) still takes the whole slot. A slot's count is its container's ItemStacks. A stack applies its effects and its ability once. An Item Stacks scaler reads the count of the item that applied the effect, so a magnitude of 5 with Multiply With Scaler grants +5 a stack. As the count changes, an equipped item's effects read it again. An effect that reads an item's stacks where no item in the project applies it reads 1, and the Problems view says so. Leveling An item has its own level on each entity that holds it, kept under the item's asset tag. Its Granted Effects take this level, and its Active Ability is granted at it. A level provider is an asset whose level range another asset follows. Link Mode: Standalone (default) keeps the item's own range. Linked To Provider takes the range from a level provider instead. Starting Level and Max Level: the item's own range, by default 1 and 4. Both are at least 1, and the Starting Level is kept within the range. Level Provider, while linked: the asset the range comes from, an Entity, Ability, Effect, Item or Attribute Set. Right-click the field to pick from one type. A link that would make a loop is refused, with an error in the Console. While no provider is set, a warning says the item uses its own range. While linked, Starting Level and Max Level show the range in use, read-only. Link Ability & Effects links the Granted Effects and the Active Ability to this item, so their per-level values follow its range. Unlink Ability & Effects removes the links that point at this item. Each asks first, and one Undo takes it back. A given item starts at its Starting Level, unless code gives it at another level. Its level then stays between that level and the Max Level. Code changes it through the entity's GAS, with SetLevel or ModifyLevel and the item's asset tag. The link serves the inspector: the Leveling section, and the scalers of effects linked to this item, read the provider's range. At runtime, the item's level comes from its own Starting Level and Max Level, even while it is linked. Tags Context Tags describe the item, such as Weapon. The changes made by effects this item applies carry them as context, and workers can filter by them. They are not applied to the entity. Granted Tags are applied to the entity while the item is equipped. Effects Granted Effects are applied to the entity while the item is equipped. Each is applied with the item as its origin, so it takes the item's level. Unequipping removes the effects this item applied. It leaves the same effect alone where something else applied it. Use Infinite effects for bonuses that last while the item is equipped. An Instant effect commits once, when the item is equipped, and unequipping doesn't undo it. A Durational effect ends when its time runs out, even while the item is still equipped. A line under each effect says how it takes its levels, and Link makes it take this item's. New, beside an empty field, makes an effect linked to this item. Abilities Active Ability: an ability the entity learns while the item is equipped. It is granted at the item's level when the item is equipped, and removed when the item is unequipped. If the entity can't take it, because of its Max Abilities or Allow Duplicate Abilities settings, the item is still equipped, without the ability. To make the ability's levels follow the item's, use Link Ability & Effects in Leveling. Components An item's components are features it carries, each a class with hooks into its life, added with the list's +. A component hears the item Given to an entity, Equipped, Unequipped and Removed, and Used, as its holder's use of the item's Active Ability ends having paid what it costs. Its context's Restoring says a moment comes from a load, which puts back what the component's earlier moments did, as the effects it applied. A kind that makes no sense twice is offered only while the item holds none of it. A component of your own derives from AbstractItemComponent and overrides the hooks it needs, each a no-op otherwise. It's the item's, shared by everything that holds it, so what it keeps for one entity's item it keeps through its context: ctx.GetState<T>(this). Auras An Aura component holds an effect on those near its holder, while it's equipped, as a banner that inspires the allies round its bearer: each a radius, whom it takes, its holder too or not, and how often it checks (EFFECTS.md). Uses A Uses component counts the uses of the item's Active Ability, each a use that paid what it costs, as a potion's sips or a wand's charges, its Uses read at the item's level. With none left, one of the item goes, at the frame's end: a stack of it, its uses whole again for the next, or the item with its last, and its ability with it. A load gives its uses whole. An item with no Active Ability never counts any, which the Problems view says. An item holds one at most. Set Bonus A Set Bonus component gives its holder a Bonus effect while it has enough of a set's pieces equipped, as two pieces of a set giving fire resistance and four a flame aura. Each piece names its Set by a tag and carries the set's bonuses, each a component with the Pieces it needs, a number field read at its holder's level. The holder's equipped pieces count each item once, and a bonus holds while they're as many as it needs, once for the holder however many pieces carry it; it comes from one of the pieces, and moves to another as that one leaves while enough stay. A load puts the bonus back with the other effects, and weighs each set once. Cues A Cues component plays what the item shows and sounds on its holder: On Equip as it's equipped, While Equipped for as long as it is, and On Use as it's used, as the ability it lends is. A load that puts an equipped item back begins its While Equipped cues and plays no burst. Each list holds cues as an effect's does (EFFECTS.md). An item holds one at most. Workers Workers are reusable behaviours, picked from a list, that react to what happens to an entity. This group is subscribed to the entity when the item is equipped, and removed when it is unequipped. Name labels the group. It holds four lists: Attribute workers run before or after an attribute changes, for example to reduce incoming damage. Impact workers inspect the changes the entity deals. Tag workers react when the entity's tags change. Analysis workers examine the frame at its end, for example to detect death. Each list's + adds an empty worker to pick a kind for. The section's import button copies a worker group from another asset. On Hit On Hit, above the workers, holds the effects the item applies as its holder's hits land, while it's equipped: a dagger's bleed, a hammer's armor break, a barrier on a kill. Each entry has: Attribute: what a hit lowers, as Health. A hit is a loss to it that the holder deals another entity. None counts the attribute playing the project's Health role (ATTRIBUTES.md), where it has one. Effects: what it applies. Each effect's own Chance to Apply rolls as it lands, and its hits set the entry off no more, so a shock it applies doesn't shock again. A hit's proc coefficient scales their chance and duration, and 0 sets nothing off (EFFECTS.md). To: the one hit (Target), or the Holder, as a barrier on a kill does. Only On Kill: only the hit that takes the attribute from above 0 to 0 or below. Impact Types: only hits of one of these types, as attacks, so a bleed's ticks, typed apart, set off nothing. None takes any hit. The Problems view warns of a type no effect in the project deals, which never matches. When: a condition read at the hit, the holder its caster and the one hit its target. Modifiers Modifiers, under On Hit, change other effects as they're made, while it's equipped: its holder's own, as a boon that adds a burst to its holder's every Chill, or those landing on it, as a cloak that halves the stuns its wearer takes. Each entry is a rule of its own or names a shared Effect Modifier asset (EFFECTS.md). Lifesteal An item gives its holder lifesteal by an effect that raises the holder's Lifesteal, the attribute the project's Lifesteal worker names as its Share, one of its Granted Effects while it's equipped, which the Lifesteal worker heals by (WORKERS.md): a vampiric mask's Infinite effect of +0.15 Lifesteal heals its wearer 15% of each blow it deals. Its Lifesteal list is gone. Local Data Local Data is a list of named values stored on the asset. Each row has a Key (a tag) and a value of a kind: Float, Int, String, Bool, Tag, Attribute, Effect, Ability, Entity, Object, MonoBehaviour or ScriptableObject, or a kind of your own, a [Serializable] class made from LocalDataValue<T>, as a point or a colour, which the row's kinds offer beside PlayForge's. A row saves its own value alone. Object fields take project assets, not scene objects. Code reads a value by its type, data.TryGet(out float range) or data.TryGet(out MyPoint point), and a number, a Float or an Int, which can scale, with data.Value.TryReadNumber(context, out float number). PlayForge doesn't read an item's Local Data itself. Your code and workers can, with item.TryGetLocalData(key, out var data). The first row with that key wins. Used By The PlayForge assets that refer to this item, each with its type icon, such as an entity that starts with it or an effect linked to it. Click a row to select the asset. The list follows the project as it changes.

guides/PROCESSES.html.title: Processes | PlayForge
guides/PROCESSES.html.summary: Processes A process is anything that runs over time under ProcessControl: an entity's GAS, a projectile, an aura's pulse, a task sequence (TASK_SEQUENCES.md), a regeneration. ProcessControl steps each from Unity's player loop, Update, FixedUpdate or LateUpdate as it asks, moves it between its states, and ends it. A Bootstrapper in the scene brings ProcessControl up. Lifecycles A process's lifecycle says how it starts and what happens when its run is done: Lifecycle Starts When its run is done Runs async For SelfTerminating Running Terminated Yes One-shot work: a projectile, a hit, a spawn RunThenWait Running Waiting Yes Work run again and again: an ability, a dialogue RequiresControl Waiting Waiting Yes Work started from outside: an ability on a key, a gated event Synchronous Running Waiting No Work every frame for good: a health bar, steering, a buff's tick An async process's RunProcess is awaited; a Synchronous one is stepped each frame at its timing instead, through WhenUpdate, WhenFixedUpdate or WhenLateUpdate. Kinds Mono processes (LazyMonoProcess, and AbstractMonoProcess under it) are MonoBehaviours: prefabs or scene objects, with Unity's components. ProcessControl makes and destroys them. Runtime processes (LazyRuntimeProcess, and AbstractRuntimeProcess under it) are plain C# classes, with no GameObject, for logic alone. A mono process's lifecycle and timing are fields in its inspector; a runtime process gives them to its base constructor. Registering one ProcessControl.Register(process).HandledBy(gas).With(data).Run(out ProcessRelay relay); relay.Pause(); // Waiting at once, out of the steps relay.Unpause(); // Running again relay.Terminate(); // ended, and cleaned up await relay.WhenTerminated(); The relay is the handle on a registered process: its state, how long it has lived, and what's done to it. A mono process's relay reaches its children too: processes on child GameObjects pause and end with it unless told not to. A mono process's object comes from an instantiator, an AbstractMonoProcessInstantiator, as a pool hands out an idle object and takes it back as the process ends. A registration can give one of its own, .InstantiatedBy(pool), which goes ahead of its handler's and the object's own; with none, the object is cloned, and destroyed as its process ends. An object whose process has ended is no longer IsInitialized, so a pool's object can run again. Pausing A pause holds a process in place, at once. A process that can hold its run says so by returning true from TryHandlePause: its run stays alive, watches relay.IsWaiting, and carries on after TryHandleResume. Any other process has its run cancelled, and a new run starts on Unpause. ProcessControl set to Waiting or ClosedWaiting pauses everything running the same way, and leaving those states sends back exactly what they stopped. A process paused on its own stays paused, and Unpause is refused until ProcessControl is back. A Terminate asked for outranks a pause. A task sequence holds its run: no stage starts or ends, its time limits stop counting, its conditions aren't checked, and the task library's waits hold, given the token their task was handed. Groups A group is a process that holds other processes, found by a tag. Each member still runs as a process of its own; the group adds what they have in common: A cap, MaxMembers, and what happens to one member more: EGroupOverflowPolicy.Reject refuses it, so RegisterWithGroup returns false, and EvictOldest ends the oldest member to make room. A data packet they share. A member joins with the group's packet unless it asks for its own (useSharedData: false) or brings one, so what one member writes, the others read. What's done to all of them at once: PauseAll, UnpauseAll, TerminateAllMembers; ForEach visits each member in the order they joined, and ForEach<T> those of a kind; GetOldest, GetNewest, TryGetFirst<T>, HasMember, MemberCount, IsFull. DetachMember takes one out without ending it. How long the group lasts: until its last member leaves, while TerminateWhenEmpty is on, as it is by default; and ending the group ends its members, while TerminateMembersOnGroupTerminate is on, as it is by default. Its events, OnMemberJoined, OnMemberLeft and OnGroupEmpty, hear its members come and go. // Made first, to configure it; or made by its first member, with no cap var buffs = new GroupProcess("Buffs", 3, EGroupOverflowPolicy.EvictOldest) { TerminateWhenEmpty = false }; ProcessControl.RegisterGroup(buffsTag, buffs, out _); ProcessControl.RegisterWithGroup(buffsTag, new TimedBuff("Haste", 6f), out var relay); if (ProcessControl.TryGetGroup(buffsTag, out var group)) group.PauseAll(); Only runtime processes join a group. The Process Group Examples sample runs each of these from a key in a scene. Logging ProcessControl's own logs are its inspector's toggles. What processes say through ForgeLog is of the Processes system, and a sequence's of Sequences (TASK_SEQUENCES.md).

guides/RECIPES.html.title: PlayForge — Recipes | PlayForge
guides/RECIPES.html.summary: PlayForge — Recipes Ten common rules, each built from PlayForge's own assets and fields, with no code. Each is in the Additional Content sample (Package Manager → PlayForge → Samples), under Recipes, a folder each. Each reads the sample's Health attribute, in Recipes/Attributes; point its fields at your own. WORKERS.md maps the workers some of them use. A curse that bursts It deals 5 each second for 3 seconds, then 30 as it ends, whether it runs out or comes off. Curse (an effect): Durational, Duration 3, Periodic Ticks on, Ticks 3; its impact -5 Health, which lands each tick. Under its impact's contained effects, Curse Burst, On Remove, landing on its Target. Curse Burst (an effect): Instant, -30 Health. A counter Each loss another entity deals its holder sets it off, and it strikes back at that one for 10. Retaliate (an ability): one stage, Apply Effects with Retaliation. Under Activation's Triggers, one trigger: Gameplay Event, the core's Impact Taken, Attribute Health, Sign Loss, Target Instigator. Retaliation (an effect): Instant, -10 Health. Its own hit is a loss to the attacker, not to its holder, so it doesn't set itself off. For a chance, as Counter Helix's 20%, set the trigger's Chance; to strike everyone near, give the ability Auto Target and leave the trigger's Target at Own. A crit A hit doubles on a 25% chance. Critical Strike (a Value Pipeline): one Chance stage, Chance 0.25, Multiplier 2, Note "critical". Crit Blow (an effect): Instant, -20 Health, its impact's Pipeline Critical Strike. The hit's breakdown notes the crit, as the combat log shows it. The stage's Roll sets pseudo-random and luck. An execute A hit that would leave its target under a fifth of its Health takes the rest. Execute (a Value Pipeline): one Execute stage, Share 0.2, Attribute Health. Culling Blow (an effect): Instant, -15 Health, its impact's Pipeline Execute. Lifesteal While it lasts, its holder heals half of each loss it deals another. Lifesteal (an attribute), the Share of the Lifesteal worker in your Forge Project's Workers, with Health in its Health role. Vampirism (an effect): Infinite, +0.5 Lifesteal, which the Lifesteal worker heals by, the one your Forge Project's Workers give every entity as a project starts, to its Health role's attribute (WORKERS.md). An effect has no lifesteal of its own: for a blow that steals more than others, an effect raises its caster's Lifesteal while it should, and an item gives it as one of its Granted Effects (ITEMS.md). Damage return While it lasts, half of each loss its holder takes goes back to the one who dealt it. Thorns (an effect): Infinite; its Worker Group, one attribute worker, Return Damage, Target Attribute Health, Share 0.5. What it returns is typed Returned, so nothing returns it again and no lifesteal heals from it. Can't die While it lasts, no blow takes its target below 1, as Shallow Grave. Undying (an effect): Durational, Duration 5; its Worker Group, one attribute worker, Can't Fall Below, Target Attribute Health, Floor 1. On hit While it's equipped, each hit its holder deals bites for 5 more. Frost Blade (an item): its On Hit, one entry, Attribute Health, Effects Frost Bite, To Target. Frost Bite (an effect): Instant, -5 Health. Frost Bite's own hit sets nothing off again. On kill While it's equipped, the hit that takes a target's Health to 0 feeds its holder 20. Reaper's Mark (an item): its On Hit, one entry, Attribute Health, Effects Feast, To Holder, Only On Kill on. Feast (an effect): Instant, +20 Health. A phase As the boss's Health falls to half, it enrages, once. Boss (an attribute set): Health 1000; in its Worker Group, one analysis worker, Threshold, Target Health, What Share, Threshold 0.5, Crossing Falling, Trigger Once on, Effects Enrage. Enrage (an effect): Infinite, granting Recipe.Enraged. The phase's own moves start from the tag: an ability with a Tag Added trigger on Recipe.Enraged, or a stage condition that reads it. The worker's Event sends a gameplay event as well, for a trigger of its own. Formulas Scaler assets for a genre's formulas, under Formulas, each named for what it computes. A field reads one with its Shared kind (SCALERS.md); each is a Stacking Curve of a count, with an a. 1 ÷ (1 + 0.06 × Armor): Reciprocal, a 0.06, of the hit's target's Armor. In a Value Pipeline's Multiply stage, a hit leaves all of itself at 0 Armor, a half at about 17, never none. 100 ÷ (100 + Armor): Reciprocal, a 0.01: a half at 100 Armor, a third at 200. −Armor: Linear, a −1. In an Add stage, a blow of 100 against 20 Armor lands as 80. 0.15 × Stacks: Linear, a 0.15, of an item's stacks, a bonus that grows by as much with each. 1 − 1 ÷ (1 + 0.15 × Stacks): Hyperbolic, a chance that nears 1 and never reaches it: 13% with one stack, 60% with ten. 0.9 ^ Stacks: Exponential, a share that falls by a tenth with each stack. The Armor ones read the Armor attribute in Formulas/Attributes, as the hit lands; point them at your own. A starter set Plain assets named for what they are, under Starter Set; the recipes above hold the rest of a starter set, a damage over time, an on hit, an on kill and a boss's phase. Each hit reads the recipes' Health. Melee Attack (an ability): Apply Effects, Melee Hit, on what it's cast at; Cooldown Melee Cooldown. Melee Hit: Instant, -10 Health. Melee Cooldown: Durational, 1 s. Bolt (an ability): the same, its Bolt Hit -25 Health, its Bolt Cooldown 3 s. Slow (an effect): Durational, 3 s, Multiply Movement Speed by 0.7, back as it ends. Shield (an effect): Durational, 5 s, +50 to Shield's current and base while it lasts; its Modifiers, one Incoming rule whose Change Impact on Health adds an Absorb stage into Shield, so each hit on its holder's Health comes off its Shield first. Give Shield's element a base of 0, between 0 and its base, so it's 0 without one. They read the Movement Speed and Shield attributes in Starter Set/Attributes.

guides/SAVING.html.title: PlayForge — Saving and Loading | PlayForge
guides/SAVING.html.summary: PlayForge — Saving and Loading ForgeSave saves an entity at rest and loads it back. ForgeSave.Capture takes what lasts on an entity into a ForgeSnapshot. ForgeSave.Restore puts it back, on the entity it came from or on a fresh one of the same kind. A snapshot is plain serializable types, so a game writes it where it likes, through JsonUtility or its own serializer. // Save ForgeSnapshot save = ForgeSave.Capture(gas, catalog); string json = JsonUtility.ToJson(save); // Load ForgeSnapshot loaded = JsonUtility.FromJson<ForgeSnapshot>(json); ForgeSave.Restore(gas, loaded, catalog); Only a hub built from an entity can be saved or loaded: a GameplayAbilitySystem with its Entity asset, or a RuntimeGameplayAbilitySystem made from an identity. The Asset Catalog A save can't hold references to assets, because a reference doesn't last from one session to the next. It names each asset by an ID instead, and an Asset Catalog finds the asset by that ID. The catalog lists attributes, effects, abilities and items. A Forge Project is the catalog of its own assets, those in its folder. Use your Forge Project, or create one with Create → PlayForge → Forge Project. Its catalog keeps itself current. Each PlayForge asset made, copied or moved into the project's folder is named as it lands, by its GUID, which stays the same when the asset is renamed or moved, and a deleted one's entry goes. An asset moved out stays named, so a save made before still finds it. The project catches up on assets it doesn't name yet as it's imported and once each editor session, so one made before PlayForge kept catalogs catches up too. Pass the project to every capture and restore. Keep Catalog Current, on the project, turns this off. Then, in the project's inspector, open the menu in its header and choose Add Its Assets, which names each PlayForge asset in the project's folder by its GUID; Add Every PlayForge Asset names every one in the Unity project. Run it again after you add assets. Code can add entries while the game runs, with catalog.Add(id, asset). An ID or an asset can be listed only once. A capture leaves out an asset the catalog doesn't name, and logs a warning. A restore does the same for an ID the catalog can't find. What a save holds Each attribute's permanent commits, as a total per retention group. Modifiers aren't saved: they come back with the effects that carry them. The levels the entity keeps: its own, and its abilities' and items'. Its own is saved as the entity's own, so a save of one kind loads onto another kind as that one's level. The abilities it knows of its own, in their slots, at their levels. Its items in order, each with its level and stacks, worn or not. Its effects, each with what applied it, its stacks, its time left and the time to its next tick, and the magnitudes its caller set. Stacks with durations of their own keep their own times. The times are kept in full, as the effect's timers keep them, so a restored effect keeps time with one that never was, to the last digit. Its loose tags, and the time scale its code set; its Time Scale attribute's is read again from the attribute. An ability that an effect or a worn item lends isn't saved on its own. It comes back with the effect or the item. A save leaves out: the entity's Local Data; its sides, which come from its asset and its registration; what an effect captured as it landed, such as a source's attribute or a roll made once. The effect captures it again as it comes back. What a load does Running abilities are interrupted, and the input buffer empties. The entity lets go of its effects, items and abilities, and the actions queued this frame are dropped. An ability it holds in the slot the save gives it stays as it is, so another entity's effect that it applied still names it. The save's abilities, items, effects, levels and commits come back. The tags compile once, and OnRestored fires. A load tells nothing as it goes: No effect is told as applied or removed, and no attribute as changed. Nothing of an effect's application runs again: not its workers, its commits on application, or its contained effects. A worn item's effects come back from the save, so wearing it again applies none. The one tag compile tells what the load changed, as any compile does. Then gas.GetCallbacks().OnRestored fires once. Listen to it to refresh what shows the entity, such as a health bar or a hotbar. The entity's attribute set has to define the attributes the save names. An attribute the catalog names but the save doesn't list loses its commits, since the entity had none when it was saved. Load between the entity's steps. A restore called from inside the entity's step or its end of frame, as from one of its callbacks, is refused with a warning, because it would empty the lists the step is going through. Load on the next frame instead. Effects from other entities An effect knows what applied it: an entity, or one of its abilities or items. When that is another entity, the save needs a name for it that lasts. Give Capture and Restore an IForgeEntityIds, which maps the game's own IDs to its entities: class Roster : IForgeEntityIds { public string IdOf(IGameplayAbilitySystem entity) => /* the game's ID for it, or null */; public IGameplayAbilitySystem Find(string id) => /* the entity, or null if it's gone */; } var save = ForgeSave.Capture(hero, catalog, roster); ForgeSave.Restore(hero, save, catalog, roster); Without IDs, or when the other entity is gone, the effect comes back as the entity's own. An entity whose abilities are in their saved slots keeps them through its load, so several entities can load in any order and their effects on each other still name the abilities that applied them. Items aren't kept that way: when several entities load together, restore those whose items applied effects first, so the others find them. Rolling back A rollback saves each step, and on a late input loads a step back and runs again. With a fixed tick (ProcessControl's Fixed Tick Rate, or a world of its own stepped by a fixed time) and the random source seeded for each step (ForgeRandom.Use), the run again lands where the first did, to the last digit of every save. Keep the saves in memory, as ForgeSnapshots: JsonUtility can move the last digit of a double as it reads one back. A load ends the abilities running, so an ability that runs over several steps isn't replayed by a load into its middle; one that ends as it activates is. Copying an entity ForgeSave.Copy(from, onto) copies what lasts on one entity onto another, as a mirror clone takes its original's state. It's a capture and a restore with no catalog and no IDs, since both entities are in the same session, so it copies assets made as the game runs too. An effect another entity applied stays that entity's, and the entity's own level goes onto the other's own. var clone = new RuntimeGameplayAbilitySystem(identity); ProcessControl.Register(clone).Run(); ForgeSave.Copy(original, clone); Versions ForgeSnapshot.Version names the save's format, and ForgeSave.Version the format this PlayForge writes. A restore refuses a save with a newer format.

guides/SCALERS.html.title: PlayForge — Scalers | PlayForge
guides/SCALERS.html.summary: PlayForge — Scalers A scaler is a value source that a magnitude field reads at a level, such as a table of damage per level. The level is the origin's, such as the level of the ability that applies an effect. Each section below matches what the inspector shows. A magnitude field A magnitude field, such as an effect's Magnitude or Duration, is a number field (ScalableFloat, or ScalableInt for a whole number). It shows its name, then its kind, then what it reads, then its field menu, which opens as wide as its items. The kind menu lists Constant, Table, By Level, Shared, × Attribute and Set By Caller at its top, then the kinds that read the game (below): Asset Part, Group, Group Impact, Local Data, Relative to a Field and Worker. It files the rest by category: the scalers of every kind under Scaler, Effect Stacks and Tracked Impact under Effect, Item Stacks under Item, and a kind of a project's own under the category it names. A field whose code declares what its context provides, with [NumberContext], offers only the kinds that can be worked out there: a targeting task's range, which has no target yet, offers no kind that reads one. Every number an asset authors is a number field, read at the level of what holds it: an ability's, as its Buffer Window and its tasks', at its level; an effect's, as its Stack Bounds' Min and Max, its Starting Stacks and a Stacks change's, at the effect's; a cue's Strength, Duration, Lifetime and Volume, for its effect as it lands; an item's Max Stack Size at its own level, and a set bonus's Pieces at its holder's; and an entity's own, as a barrier's Decay Per Second, an attribute set's Snap Interval, an aura's Interval and a worker's Threshold, Floor, Share, Every Ticks, Tick Pause or Required Weight, at the entity's or the change's. A level, a pointer's button, an order, a priority among configs and a log's size stay whole numbers, as do a kind's and a scaler's own numbers. A folded field's line shows a number field by what it reads, as "Uses 3". Constant: the field reads its number, with its unit beside it, as Tick Every's "1 s". A field that used to read its scaler, and has none, reads 0, and a warning says so. Table: the field reads one value for each level, exactly: level 1 the first, level 4 the 4th, and a level past the last the last, as Laguna Blade's 450, 600 and 750. The range it gives shows beside the kind, as "6–8 s", or "-25 to -10" where it goes below 0. Its values sit in a row under it, with no curve. By Level: the field reads its values spread over a level range, as points on a curve, a level between two reading between them (below). It's the same number by level as a Table, read another way, so choosing one for the other keeps its values; one saved reading exactly shows as a Table, and nothing saved changes. SPREADSHEETS.md writes a project's Tables and By Levels to a spreadsheet and reads them back. Shared: the field reads a Scaler asset (below). The other kinds work out a value from the values or from the entity: × Attribute reads an attribute of the caster or the target, its current, its base, what's missing of it (base − current) or its share of its base (current ÷ base), which the menu starts as the field's number times it, all of it or only some of its retention groups (below), and reads it as its attribute's role says, a Bonus Share as 1 + x and a Resistance as 1 − x, or as its Read As says, Clamped keeps a number within bounds, Conditional reads one number where a condition holds and another where it doesn't, Randomized rolls a random value, Threshold steps at thresholds, and Fixed Value is one number. Stacking Curve turns a Count, as an item's stacks or an attribute, into its number by a Curve and its Coefficient, a: Linear, a × n, as 15% a stack; Hyperbolic, 1 − 1 / (1 + a × n), a chance that nears 1 and never reaches it, 13% with one stack and 60% with ten at 0.15; Reciprocal, 1 / (1 + a × n), as what Dota's armor leaves of a hit at 0.06; Inverse, a / n, as a wind-up an attack speed shortens; and Exponential, a to the n. Its Plus is added after, 1 making a share a multiplier. Effect Stacks reads the stack count of the effect's own container, and Item Stacks that of the item that applied it (ITEMS.md); each reads 1 where there's nothing stacked. An attribute set's values use the cached kinds, which read other attributes as the entity's values change. Set By Caller reads a value the code passes in. It checks one thing: whether what the number is read in holds a value under exactly its Key. Code sets one on an effect's spec before applying it (spec.SetByCaller(tag, value)), on an ability activation's data (data.SetByCaller(tag, value)), which each effect the ability makes takes and the ability's tasks read, or on the data that spawns a process (EFFECTS.md). Only the key itself matches, not a tag above or below it in the tag tree, and a value set to 0 is a value. Where none is set, the field reads the kind's Default; its summary says both, as "the caller's Damage, else 0". A Threshold lists its thresholds, each a Level and an optional Tier name, with the Value it reads from that level up under them, a number of any kind; below every threshold it reads its Default Value. A Conditional has a condition, When, and two numbers, True Value and False Value: it reads True where the condition holds, and False where it doesn't, or where it has none. Its summary says all three, as "−0.1 × Target's Health (base) if Target's Health < 0.3 × Target's Health (base), else 0". A condition picks its kind from a menu, as a number does, and says itself in a line: Tag: whether the caster or the target holds a tag, counted by its weight, so a tag granted twice counts twice; Attribute: an attribute of the caster or the target, its current, its base, what's missing of it or its share of its base, compared with a number, as 0.3 × the target's base Health, or a share above 0.9 for "above 90%"; Level: the level, or how far up its range it is, from 0 to 1, compared with a number; Compare Numbers: one number compared with another; Always and Never; and under Logic, All Of, Any Of and Not, which join others. All Of none holds; Any Of none doesn't. Where what the number is read in lacks what a condition reads, as a target's tag where there's no target, the condition doesn't hold, and neither does Not it. A Clamped keeps its Value between its Min Value and Max Value, three numbers of any kind; one made in the inspector clamps a value by level. A Randomized scaler's Variance is a kind of its own: Percentage, up or down by a Share of its value; Flat, by an Amount; Multiplier, times one between its Min and its Max; or one of your own, as two dice, a [Serializable] class made from AbstractVariance that overrides Vary, Lowest and Highest. Its numbers read the variance as their object, so a Share can widen by level and a Max can be 3 × its Min. A scaler's own numbers read the scaler as their object: a Clamped's Max Value can be Relative to a Field, 2 × its Min Value, whatever field the Clamped is in. A Group joins several numbers as one. It lists its members, each an Operation then its Scaler, which can be any kind. The members that Add are added up, that sum is multiplied by each member that Multiplies and divided by each that Divides, one that reads 0 dividing nothing, then each Flat Bonus is added on, in whatever order they're listed, so (5 + Caster's Strength) × 2 + 3 is one number, and 1.7 ÷ Caster's Attack Speed another, and a first member needn't add. Members that multiply or divide with none that adds work on 0, and the Group says so. A member that Overrides gives the group's value alone; where several do, the group's policy picks the highest, the lowest, their average, the first or the last, and Ignore sets them aside. A Group has no values per level. With no members, or none that holds a kind, it's no kind at all, so its field reads its number, as a Constant does. Kinds that read the game, each with a summary that says what it reads: Local Data reads the number under a Key in Local Data: Its Own, what the number belongs to, as its ability's or its item's asset, or the Caster's or the Target's as the entity holds it. Where there's no number under the key it reads its Default. A hero's attack range kept in its Local Data is one field read by every ability. The entry's number can scale too, read where the kind reads it: Its Own in the number's context, the Caster's or the Target's at that entity's own level. One that reads its own key stops at the Default. Relative to a Field reads another number field of the same object, picked from a menu of them, and the field's number joins it as Combine says: a Clamped scaler's Max can be 2 × its Min, and a stack bound's Max its Min + 3. The other field is read in the same context, so a relative Max follows a Min that scales by level. A field offers this kind where its code hands its object over as it reads (below). Tracked Impact, under Effect, reads what an effect has dealt: its Last impact, its Total, or its impact Count. Whose: This Effect, as a burn that grows by its own tick count; An Effect on the caster or the target, by its asset; or Effects Tagged there, added up. An impact is as it landed, after the target's workers, and signed, so damage is negative; By Size reads it positive, as a heal of half a blow wants. Before an effect's first impact, and after a load, it reads 0. Group Impact reads one retention group's part of an attribute on the caster or the target, as "Caster's Strength (Bonus)": the Strength items add, and none of the hero's own. Retention groups in any attribute read: × Attribute, the Attribute condition, a relative attribute worker's Relative To and the Threshold worker each have Groups: All, the whole value, as before; Only These, as a bonus of the items' Strength reads their group; or All But These, as a bonus of a hero's own damage leaves its items' out. A group names the groups under it too, so Items takes Items.Ring. The read says which: "Caster's Strength (Items)", "Caster's Attack Damage (all but Items)". Asset Part finds effects, abilities or items on the caster or the target by a tag, and reads a part of them. An effect matches by its asset tag, a context tag or a tag it grants, and an ability or an item by its asset tag or a context tag; a tag under the one given matches too. Of an Effect: its Count, Stacks, Level, Last Impact, Total Impact, Impact Count, Duration Remaining, Duration, Time Until Tick, or a Worker Value, what that effect's workers answer under a key. Of an Ability: its Count, Level, Is Active, Is on Cooldown, or Cooldown Remaining. Of an Item: its Count, Stacks, Level, or Is Equipped. Among says how several that match read as one: their Sum, the First, the Highest or the Lowest. A true-or-false part reads 1 or 0, so its sum is how many are so. Where none matches, a count reads 0 and any other part the Default. Worker asks workers for a number under a Key: This Effect's own workers, or the Caster's or the Target's. Where none answers it reads its Default. See Asking a worker, below. Choosing a kind is one Undo step. A constant made a Table or By Level keeps its number as its first level's value. With more than one asset selected, the field edits each asset's own field. Kinds that differ show as mixed, and choosing one gives it to each field, from that field's own value; a field of that kind keeps its scaler. Levels and Make Constant work on each field's own values, and a count, range or curve the fields disagree on shows as mixed. Save as Scaler Asset waits for one asset. A kind other than Constant shows a one-line summary of what the field reads under its row, as "0.3 × Target's Health (base)", then Combine, how the field joins its number with the scaler: Scaler reads the scaler's value, Scaler + Number and Scaler × Number add or multiply the field's number, and Number Only reads the number. A whole-number field, such as Ticks, also shows its Rounding: Floor, Ceil, or Round, to the nearest, a half away from zero. A field whose unit is "%" stores 0.3 and shows and takes it as 30%. A kind its field can't work out, as one copied from a field that has a target into one that hasn't, says so under the field, and the Problems window lists it; it reads the field's number. The field menu holds the items below. A scaler field of its own, as a Group member's, has the same menu, and its kind menu files its kinds by category, as a number field's does. Save as Scaler Asset…: a name and a folder, then Save and Use, which saves the field's scaler as a Scaler asset and makes the field share it. Scaler Assets: a submenu of the project's Scaler assets, the one the field shares checked. The field shares the one you pick. Import Values…: a window that lists the Scaler assets and the other assets' fields with values per level. Pick one to compare its values with the field's, level by level, with both curves, then Copy Values. A shorter table's last value holds for the levels past its end, and the window says which levels those are. One Undo takes it back. Quick Fill…: fills the table from a pattern: Same Value, Straight Line, Slow Then Fast and Fast Then Slow with a Strength, Steps, Add Each Level, Multiply Each Level, Ease In and Out, or a Custom Curve you draw, from one value to another. Rounding makes the values whole numbers or rounds them to a Step. A preview shows the values as the table will, with their curve, and one Undo takes them back. On a scaler spread over levels it fills the points, as many as Points says, and the preview shows what each level reads between them. Make Constant: the field reads a number again, the value its first level read. A scaler field of its own, with no number, becomes a Fixed Value of that value. Values per level A scaler's settings sit on a shaded block under its field, so they read as the scaler's among the fields around them. A kind shows only what it reads: a Fixed Value shows its value, and a Randomized scaler its variance, then the values its base value comes from. A kind's field that applies only to some of its settings shows only for them, as an Asset Part's worker key for an effect's Worker Value. Values: Per Level or Spread Over Levels. A Table reads Per Level and By Level spreads, as their kinds say, so they have no choice here; a scaler of another kind with values for each level chooses. Per Level: one value per level, ten levels to a row. Level 1 reads the first value, level 4 the 4th, and a level past the end reads the last. Spread Over Levels: the values are points on a curve over a level range, and a level between two points reads between them. Three values, 10, 20 and 30, spread over levels 1 to 5 read 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30. The points are numbered, and under them each level shows what it reads. A scaler you make in the inspector starts Per Level. The scalers saved before the choice existed spread, so they read as they did. Levels, Per Level: an asset with a level provider, as an ability, or an effect linked to one, follows the provider's levels, as Fireball's levels (1–4), with a value for each. A level past the scaler's values shows the last in secondary text; type there to give it a value of its own. Own levels gives the scaler a count of its own. An asset whose levels come from whatever uses it, as an unlinked effect, an attribute set or a Scaler asset, shows the count alone. A new level takes the last value. Over Levels, spread: the provider's levels, Own levels up to the scaler's own Max Level, or the provider's up to a level: its levels, up to the Max Level, so the values reach the last at the lower of the Max Level and the provider's last level, and a level past it reads the last value. Points: how many values. Between Points, spread: Steps, Straight Line or Smooth Curve. A read-only curve beside the table shows the values, and spread, the curve they make. Its tooltip reads them, as "6 at level 1, rising to 8 at level 5". Behaviours: rules that adjust the value the scaler works out, in order. Quick Fill fills the levels the table shows. Nothing changes a scaler's values while it's drawn: its table keeps its length until you change it. Writing your own scaler A scaler of your own derives from AbstractScaler, or from AbstractCachedScaler for an attribute set's values, and has a public constructor with no parameters. The Kind menu lists it by its name without "Scaler", as Damage Curve for DamageCurveScaler. Its inspector draws: Each field it adds, public or [SerializeField], as Unity draws the field's type, through any property drawer you write for that type. The fields of an abstract base of your own draw too. [HideInInspector] keeps a field out, and [ForgeShowWhen(nameof(Mode), EMode.Curved)] shows one only while another field, an enum or a bool, holds one of the values given. The parts every scaler has, as its Parts say: its values per level (EScalerParts.LevelValues), the level range they spread over (EScalerParts.LevelRange), and its behaviours (EScalerParts.Behaviours). Unless you override it, a scaler reads all three, or its behaviours alone where its UseScalingOptions() returns false. Override Parts to say what yours reads, as a scaler that reads only an attribute returns EScalerParts.Behaviours. Parts can follow the scaler's own fields, as one that reads its values per level in one mode alone. A kind of number of your own is simpler: derive from NumberKind and override its one method, Evaluate(in NumberContext context), which reads what the field's site has: context.Caster, context.Target, context.Level, the caller's magnitudes, Local Data, an attribute on either side, and more; context.Has(...) says which. Describe() gives the field's summary, as "the distance to the target". [NumberKind("Distance to Target", Reads = NumberReads.Caster | NumberReads.Target)] names it and says what it reads, so a field offers it only where it can be worked out; where it can't, the field reads its number. [ForgeMenu("Space")] files it in the kind menu. A kind is a scaler, so it also works in an effect's magnitude and inside a Group or a Conditional, and its fields draw as a scaler's do. Test one without an effect: number.Evaluate(NumberContext.For(caster, target, level)). A kind is saved by its class's name, so renaming the class needs Unity's [MovedFrom]. PlayForge's own kinds, Local Data, Tracked Impact, Asset Part and the rest, are written this way, in Runtime/PlayForge/Numbers/Kinds. A condition of your own, for a Conditional, is the same: derive from GameplayCondition, override Evaluate(in NumberContext context) to say whether it holds and Describe() for its line, and name it with [GameplayCondition("Target Is Caster", Reads = NumberReads.Caster | NumberReads.Target)]; the condition menu offers it, and condition.Holds(context) reads it. A kind or a condition that holds numbers reads them with itself as their owner, MaxValue.Evaluate(context, this), and passes Initialize(carrier) on to them, so a number in it captures what it captures as an effect's spec is made. PlayForge's are in Runtime/PlayForge/Numbers/Conditions. A number field in your own code A field of your own is one line, and a float converts to it: [Tooltip("How far it reaches")] [NumberContext(NumberReads.Level | NumberReads.Caster, Unit = "m")] [NumberMin(0)] public ScalableFloat Range = 20f; Read it with Range.Evaluate(context), with a NumberContext built Of what the code has: an effect's spec, an activation's data, a worker's context, an entity, a cue or a process. Range.Evaluate(context, this) also hands the field's object over, which is what Relative to a Field reads; a field read that way declares NumberReads.Owner, or NumberReads.All, and its kind menu then offers that kind. [Tooltip] shows on the field's name. [NumberMin(0)], [NumberMax(10)] and [NumberRange(0, 1)] limit the constant typed in the inspector, and a range sets it on a slider. On a field whose unit is "%" the limit is in what the field stores, so [NumberRange(0, 1)] is 0% to 100%, and a whole-number field takes the whole numbers inside the limits. They limit the constant alone: a number of another kind is worked out as the game runs, so where what it reads must stay inside limits, give it the Clamped kind or clamp what the code reads. In a kind of your own, as an ability task, a targeting task or a scaler, [ShownWhen(nameof(UsePhysics))] shows a field only while a toggle of the same object is on, and [ShownWhen(nameof(Mode), (int)EMode.Area)] only while an enum is one of the values, as a targeting task's Detection Layers show under Use Physics. A task reads its numbers with Read(number, data), at its ability's level. Every kind of your own, a task, a worker, a component, a cue, a kind of number or a condition, takes [ForgeMenu("Path/Sub", Name = "...", Description = "...")]: its picker files it under the submenus its path names, a slash nesting them; Name replaces its class's name in the picker and in its field; and Description is what the picker's Context says while it's highlighted. A path holds for the classes made from the one that names it, and [ForgeMenu("")] puts a kind at the top whatever its base names. Unity's own [Min] and [Range] don't work on a number field: Unity gives the field to that attribute's drawer, which draws "Use Range with float or int" where the number was. As scripts load, the console names each number field that has one, with the attribute to use in its place. Asking a worker A number can't count or remember; a worker can. So a number of the Worker kind asks workers for a value under a key, and any worker answers by implementing INumberWorker: public class OverkillWorker : AbstractEffectWorker, INumberWorker { public Tag Key; public bool TryGetNumber(Tag key, in NumberContext context, out float value) { value = 0f; if (key != Key) return false; // not a key it knows: the next worker is asked var state = (context.Carrier as GameplayEffectSpec)?.GetWorkerState<State>(this); value = state?.Overkill ?? 0f; return true; } } An effect's workers answer about one application of their effect. A worker is one object on its effect's asset, shared by every application, so what it counts for each is kept on the spec: ctx.GetState<State>(this) in its events, and spec.GetWorkerState<State>(this) as it answers. An entity's workers, those its worker groups give it, answer about the entity. A worker group installs the ones that answer as it's given, and code that adds a worker itself calls NumberWorkers.Provide(entity, worker). The first worker that answers the key gives the value. Where none does, the number reads its Default. Any number field can ask: an effect's magnitude, a task's range, a threshold. Code can ask too, with NumberWorkers.TryAsk. An Asset Part's Worker Value asks the workers of each effect it finds. The Attribute Change effect worker is one that answers. It notes an attribute as each application of its effect begins, and answers how much the attribute has Lost, Gained or Changed since, or what it was At Start. With Every Ticks above 0 it answers only on each Nth tick, and 0 on the others. A curse that deals 5 a second, and every fourth second a quarter of the health its target has lost since it landed, from every source, is one periodic effect: its first impact is −5, and its second is a Worker number, −0.25 × the worker's answer, with the worker watching the target's Health, Lost, Every Ticks 4. Scaler assets A Scaler asset (Create → PlayForge → Scaler) holds one scaler that many fields can use. A field of the Shared kind reads its Asset's scaler, so an edit to the asset changes every field that uses it, with nothing to copy or propagate. Open shows the asset in a window of its own. Under the field, the asset's curve shows beside its range, as "6–8, levels 1–5", and how many fields share it. A field adjusts the shared values only through its own number and Combine: Scaler × Number with a number of 1.5 reads the asset's values times 1.5, as in Fire Duration × 1.5. The asset's own inspector shows its name, its kind and how many fields use it, its Name, which renames it, as The Forge and the field menus list it, its Description, its Values, and Used By: each field that shares it, by its asset and field. Click a row to select the asset. In The Forge, its summary says its description, its kind, what it reads and how many fields use it. Its Try section reads it at each level of a range, Levels 1 to 5 to start, as an effect's Levels does: a row of what it gives at each, and under it the parts behind the level picked. It reads against a stand-in Caster and Target and a Caller, each with a row for what the scaler asks of it, found as it reads: an attribute on its side, whether the side Has it, its current and its base; and a key the caller sets, whether it's Set and its value, unset reading the scaler's default. A side's Entity fills its attributes from what that entity's attribute set starts each at, at its starting level, and one the set doesn't give, it lacks. A stand-in holds attributes alone, so a number that reads an effect, an item, a tag, a retention group's part or Local Data reads as on an entity with none of them. What's typed is kept for the session, never in the asset. ScalerTry does the same in code: new ScalerTry { From = 1, To = 5 }.Read(scaler). Any magnitude field can share a Scaler asset. An attribute set's element shares one whose scaler is a cached kind, and its Scaler Assets lists only those. A Scaler asset can't hold a Shared scaler of its own. A field whose asset is missing reads as a field with no scaler, and an element whose asset is missing reads its root value. A chain of shared scalers that comes back to its own asset stops after eight steps, rather than run forever. The Scaler asset was the Scaler Template, whose link and sync settings nothing read, so those settings are gone. So are the old scaler window's curve editor and import window: a scaler's values are its table, and Import Values compares them before it copies.

guides/SPREADSHEETS.html.title: PlayForge — Spreadsheets | PlayForge
guides/SPREADSHEETS.html.summary: PlayForge — Spreadsheets Games balance in spreadsheets: a column of damage by level, a row of stats for each item. PlayForge writes its numbers by level and its items' stats to CSV, which any spreadsheet opens, and reads a sheet back, listing each change before it makes it. The Forge's window menu (its tab's ⋮) holds them under Spreadsheets: Export Numbers… writes a sheet of every number by level in the active Forge Project; Export Selected Numbers… the selected assets' alone. Export Item Stats… writes a sheet of every item's stats; Export Selected Item Stats… the selected items'. Import… reads a sheet back, of either kind, and opens the import window. A sheet is UTF-8, marked so, as Excel and Google Sheets open it. In code: ForgeSpreadsheets.NumbersOf(assets) and StatsOf(items) give a sheet's text, and ForgeSpreadsheets.Read(csv) what it would change. Numbers by level A row for each number whose kind is a Table or By Level (SCALERS.md), of every asset, and of each Scaler asset, whose table its fields share: Asset Tag Name Field Kind Level 1 Level 2 Level 3 Effect.LagunaBlade Laguna Blade Impact Specification › Magnitude Table -450 -600 -750 AttributeSet.Hero Hero Attributes › Health › Base Table 500 560 620 Field is the number's place in the asset, its parts as the inspector names them; a list's element is named by the attribute it names, as an attribute set's Health, or else by its place from 1, as Additional Impacts 2. The levels are what the number reads at each level: its values combined with its number as its field says, so a table of 450, 600 and 750 read times -1 is -450, -600 and -750. Reading one back sets the values so it reads the row. A number that reads its number alone, or a kind of another sort, as × Attribute, has no row. Item stats A row for each item, and a column for each attribute its granted effects add to: Asset Tag Name Armor Health Item.Ring Ring 5 10/15/20 Item.Band Band A cell is the number the item's effect adds to the attribute, or one for each level, as 10/15/20. An item whose effects add to an attribute twice leaves that cell empty: set each in a sheet of numbers. Reading a sheet back sets the effect's number: a constant's, or a Table's values; one for each level makes a constant a Table. An empty cell changes nothing. Reading a sheet back A row names its asset both ways: by its asset tag, which stays as files move and are renamed, and by its name, which reads well in a spreadsheet. A row with a tag finds the asset with that tag; a row with none finds the one asset of that name. These are reported, and their rows left: a tag no asset has, or a name no asset has, or one that two assets share (give that row its tag); a field the asset hasn't got, or a kind a sheet can't set; an item with no effect adding to a column's attribute; a cell that isn't a number; two rows setting one shared effect's number to different values. The import window lists each change: the asset, the field, what it reads now and what it will. Each is ticked; untick one to leave it. The rows that can't be read sit under a fold. Import makes the ticked changes as one Undo step. A sheet read back just as it was written changes nothing.

guides/TASK_SEQUENCES.html.title: Task Sequences | PlayForge
guides/TASK_SEQUENCES.html.summary: Task Sequences A task sequence is a workflow over time, built in code: stages run one after another, each a set of tasks run together. An ability runs as one, and so can anything with steps: a projectile's flight, a channel, a cutscene, a tutorial, a boss's phases. A sequence runs as a process (PROCESSES.md), so ProcessControl starts, pauses and ends it like any other. The Task Sequence Examples sample shows every part of this page in code, and a component that runs any example from a scene. The parts Sequence: its stages, in order, with what holds for all of them: its name, its conditions, a timeout or a longest run, whether it repeats, and the handlers that hear it end. Stage: its tasks, run together, and its policy, which says when the stage is done: when all its tasks are (WhenAll, the default), any one (WhenAny), or a number of them (WhenN). A stage can hold stages of its own (SubStage), or be a branch that picks one stage by a condition. Task: one unit of work, awaited (Task), done at once (Do), stepped a frame at a time (SyncTask), or a class of its own (ISequenceTask, or SequenceTaskBase and SyncSequenceTaskBase to start from). Injection: a change to the run from outside its tasks: interrupt it, skip a stage, jump to one, break a repeat. A condition injects one when its predicate holds, checked each frame. Chain: sequences run one after another with one data packet. Building one var cast = TaskSequenceBuilder.Create("Fireball") .WithMaxDuration(5f) .Stage(stage => stage .WithName("Wind Up") .Task((data, token) => SequenceTaskLibrary.PlayAnimationState(animator, "Cast", token))) .Stage(stage => stage .WithName("Flight") .Task((data, token) => SequenceTaskLibrary.ArcTowards(fireball, target, 20f, 2f, token))) .Stage(stage => stage .WithName("Impact") .Do(data => ForgeLog.Info("Fireball lands"))) .BuildSequence(); cast.RegisterAndRun(SequenceDataPacket.SceneRoot()); Build gives the definition, which a TaskSequence runs and a synced runner is built from; BuildSequence gives the sequence itself, and BuildSyncRunner a synced runner (below). A static method marked [TaskSequenceMethod] that returns a sequence, a chain or a definition appears in an ability's sequence dropdown, and in a TaskSequenceReference field; an ability runs a chain as a process too, which asks its conditions each frame. A task reads and writes the run's data packet, a SequenceDataPacket: what started the run put its caster, targets and values there, and a task can leave values for the stages after it (SetPrimary, GetPrimary). Waiting Delays: Delay(seconds) is a stage of its own that waits; DelayUntil and DelayWhile wait on a predicate, and WaitUntil is a stage that does. SyncDelay waits inside a stage, as one of its tasks. The library's waits, inside a task: SequenceTaskLibrary.Delay, WaitFrames, Yield, WaitUntil and WaitWhile. The player's input, read through ForgeInput, so a game's own input or a test's stands in: WaitForKey, WaitForAnyKey, which returns the key pressed, and WaitForPointer. Each of the library's waits holds while its sequence is paused, and a press while it's paused isn't heard. A task that keeps time itself should read SequenceTaskLibrary.DeltaTime(token), a step of its run's clock (below), which is 0 while the sequence is paused. A task that links its token, to cancel a wait of its own without its stage, links it through TaskSequenceRuntime.CreateLinkedTokenSource(token), whose token belongs to the task's run, so a wait on it keeps the run's clock and holds while the run is paused. A token that CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource links belongs to no run, so its waits go by the game's clock and don't hold. Dispose the source once done, as any: .Task(async (data, token) => { // Cancelled with the stage, or on its own through charge.Cancel(), and by the run's clock either way using var charge = TaskSequenceRuntime.CreateLinkedTokenSource(token); await SequenceTaskLibrary.Delay(1.5f, charge.Token); }) Repeating WithRepeat(true) on the builder repeats the whole sequence until it's interrupted. WithRepeat(true) on a stage repeats the stage until it's broken (data.BreakStageRepeat(), StopRepeatWhen), skipped or interrupted; WithRepeatAndDelay(seconds) waits between repeats. WithRepeat(3) on a stage runs it three times in all, then the sequence moves on. A break, a skip or an interrupt still ends it sooner. A stage's OnRepeat hears each repeat, and runtime.GetRepeatCount(stage) says how many runs are done. Changing the run From a task, through its data packet: data.SkipStage(); // end this stage, on to the next data.SkipAndMaintain(); // on to the next, leaving this one's tasks running data.JumpToStage("Impact"); // or by index data.RestartSequence(); data.BreakStageRepeat(); data.Interrupt(); // end the run data.SetStageTimeout(2f); // this stage gets two seconds, then it's skipped From outside, through the sequence or its runtime: Inject(injection), Interrupt(), SkipCurrentStage(). By a condition, checked each frame: InterruptWhen, SkipStageWhen on the sequence, SkipWhen and StopRepeatWhen on a stage, and InjectWhen for any injection. A condition fires once or every time it holds. A stage's condition is asked each frame by the process, so where a repeating stage's round ends, the next may have begun before StopRepeatWhen hears its predicate hold: a break from a task or from OnRepeat stops at the round exactly. SkipAndMaintain keeps the stage current as it's called running on; called again later, it keeps that later one. InjectStageLocal(injection, stage) asks the given stage's permissions, and the injection acts on the current stage. What may change a run is the sequence's to say: AllowInjections(types), AllowOnlyInterrupt() and DisallowInjections(), on the sequence or a stage. A critical stage (WithCriticalFlag(true)) refuses every injection but those it names (WithCriticalAllowedInjections), and OnCriticalSectionExited hears the last critical stage end. Time limits and endings WithTimeout(seconds, injection) injects when the time is up, a skip by default; WithMaxDuration(seconds) ends the run, or the stage, at its longest. OnTimeout and OnMaxDuration hear them. OnException hears a task's throw, and says whether the run goes on. OnComplete hears the run end and whether it finished; OnTerminate hears it end however it does. A stage has its own OnInit, OnRepeat and OnTerminate. Clocks A run's time is its clock's: its waits and delays, its timeouts and longest runs, its ElapsedTime, the library's tweens and its synced tasks all go by it. A run takes the first clock it finds: its own, runtime.Clock, which whatever runs it sets: a chain's Clock, a TaskSequenceProcess's, or an ability's Run Sequence task's pick, so a packet others share keeps its own; its packet's, data.Clock, which whatever starts the run sets; its sequence's own, WithClock(clock) on the builder; its packet's owner's: an ability's caster's own clock, its time scale times the game's; the game's, GameClock.Instance, which reads the clock in force, ForgeTime.Clock, as it's asked. // A pause menu's runs while the game's time stands var menu = TaskSequenceBuilder.Create("Menu").WithClock(UnscaledClock.Instance) /* … */; // A finisher's slow motion: every sequence on the clock slows, speeds up or stops with it var slowMotion = new ScaledClock(0.25f); var finisher = TaskSequenceBuilder.Create("Finisher").WithClock(slowMotion) /* … */; // One run on an entity's time, from its packet var data = SequenceDataPacket.Default(); data.Clock = gas.GetClock(); UnscaledClock.Instance reads the game's time without its time scale. A ScaledClock runs at a Scale of its own over its Source, the clock in force unless it's given one, and counts its own Time through each change of scale. An entity's EntityClock is a clock as any other is. A clock of your own implements IForgeClock, and is read as it is. The clocks above read the clock in force, so a world of its own's steps and the fixed tick still drive them; one that reads Unity's time itself doesn't follow them. runtime.Clock is a run's clock, and TaskSequenceRuntime.ClockOfRun(token) the clock of the run a task's token belongs to. A synced runner takes its sequence's clock (runner.Clock), a packet's before it (runner.ClockFor(data)), and runner.Step(data) steps by it. An inspector picks a clock with an AbstractClockChoice field, [SerializeReference]: None, which leaves a run the clock it would have had, the Caster's, the Game's, Unscaled, or Scaled, a pace of its own over the clock it picks, the caster's unless it picks another. A [Serializable] class of your own made from it is offered beside them, its ClockFor(data) giving the clock for a run on a packet. An ability's Run Sequence task has one, which gives the sequence it runs a clock of its own and leaves the ability's other tasks the caster's; so do the Task Sequence Examples' components, and a Sequence cue, whose run goes by its pick, else the sequence's own clock, else that of the one the cue plays on. Under ProcessControl's fixed tick, a sequence waits for the next tick, and the ticks run on the game's time, so they stand with it. A clock that runs while the game's time stands says so, FollowsTicks false as the unscaled clock's is, and its sequences wait for Unity's frames instead. Code outside a sequence awaits ForgeTick.Next(clock) for the next step of a clock's time. A synced sequence run as a process steps with ProcessControl, by its ticks, whatever its clock. Running one RegisterAndRun(data), or ProcessControl.Register(sequence).With(data).Run(), runs it as a process: it shows in the Debugger, pauses with ProcessControl, and ends with its scene. await sequence.Run(data, token) runs it in place, from code that's async already, and TryRun says whether it finished. CreateRuntime gives the runtime that runs it, to pause, resume, inject and read: its stage, its time, whether it finished, what it threw. TaskSequenceProcess wraps a sequence, a chain or a synced runner as a process of a lifecycle and timing given. Chains // countdown and fight are TaskSequences; the last is built in place var round = countdown.Then(fight).Then(builder => builder.WithName("Results").Stage(stage => stage.Do(ShowResults))); await round.Run(SequenceDataPacket.SceneRoot()); A chain runs its sequences in order with one data packet; it can repeat, pause and resume, skip its current sequence, or be interrupted, and takes conditions of its own (InterruptWhen, SkipSequenceWhen). From inside, data.Chain is the chain, and data.InterruptChain() ends it. Synced sequences A synced runner is the same sequence stepped a frame at a time, with no async: a process with the Synchronous lifecycle calls its Step each frame. It suits what runs for good, a patrol, a regeneration, a bob, and costs nothing but the calls. using SyncSeq = FarEmerald.PlayForge.SyncSequenceTaskLibrary; runner = TaskSequenceBuilder.Create("Regenerate") .WithRepeat(true) .Stage(stage => stage.Task(SyncSeq.Delay(1f))) .Stage(stage => stage.Do(_ => Heal(5))) .BuildSyncRunner(); // In the process's WhenUpdate: a step of its clock, or Step(data, deltaTime) for a time of your own runner.Step(data); A synced task works in an async sequence too, stepped once a frame and held while the sequence is paused. Its first step comes in the frame its stage starts, so SyncSequenceTaskLibrary.Yield waits no frame there; the async Yield does. A synced runner runs stages, their tasks, the three policies, repeats with or without a count, critical stages and a stage's longest run. A sub-stage, a branch, a condition, the sequence's own timeout or longest run, or an async task it can't, and building a runner from a sequence that holds any says so. It's changed by hand: Interrupt, SkipStage, JumpToStage, BreakStageRepeat and Reset. The libraries SequenceTaskLibrary has tasks to await inside a stage's Task, each taking the task's token, and SyncSequenceTaskLibrary the same tasks as ISequenceTasks for a synced runner, or for any stage: Kind Tasks Position MoveTo, MoveBy, MoveLocalTo, MoveAlongPath, ArcTo, Dash; following a transform, MoveTowards, ArcTowards, Orbit, MoveAlongPathToTarget Rotation RotateTo, RotateBy, LookAt, and LookAtTracking, which follows Scale ScaleTo, PunchScale, and TransformTo, position, rotation and scale at once Looks FadeAlpha, ColorTo, MaterialColorTo, MaterialFloatTo Sound and animation PlayAndWait, FadeVolume, PlayAnimationState, LerpAnimFloat UI Toolkit SlideElement, FadeElement, ScaleElement, ColorElement, each with a …To from where the element is; PunchScaleElement, WidthTo, HeightTo, TypeText, TypeTextSkippable Any value Lerp, LerpFloat, LerpVector3, LerpColor Waiting Delay, WaitFrames, Yield, WaitUntil, WaitWhile, WaitForKey, WaitForAnyKey, WaitForPointer Only the async library has ArcForce, which flies a Rigidbody by physics between FixedUpdates, whatever a runner's timing; ArcTo moves a transform along the same arc, in either. IsPaused(token) and DeltaTime(token) read the run that holds the token, which a synced task has none of. A timed task takes an AnimationCurve for its easing, ends exactly on its value, and ends at once for a time of 0 or less. Logging What a sequence says goes through ForgeLog, under its own system, Sequences: a handler's throw as an error, and, where a sequence's or a chain's logging is on (WithInjectionLogging, a chain's WithLogging), what it does as information. Preferences > PlayForge > Logging sets the quietest message every system logs, and ForgeLog.SetLevel(ForgeLog.ESystem.Sequences, …) gives the sequences a level of their own, to hear more or less of them than the rest.
