guides/TESTING.html.summary: PlayForge — Testing Your Content A game's abilities, effects and items are easiest to trust when a test plays them as the game does: a burn's ticks landing over its second, a ring's armor while it's held, a cast paying its cost. PlayForge's test kit is the assembly FarEmerald.PlayForge.Testing, in the package's TestKit folder, which a project's own tests reference. It brings up a live PlayForge for each test, steps it a frame at a time, makes entities on either hub, and plays them; and after each test it checks what must always hold, and takes it all down again, so tests run in any order. Setting up The kit is compiled wherever the Test Framework package (com.unity.test-framework) is installed, as its own test runner is. In a test assembly of the project's (an assembly definition whose Define Constraints hold UNITY_INCLUDE_TESTS, referencing nunit.framework.dll), add to Assembly Definition References: FarEmerald.PlayForge and FarEmerald.PlayForge.Testing; UniTask; UnityEngine.TestRunner and UnityEditor.TestRunner. The kit's tests are PlayMode tests, as they step the real player loop: give the assembly every platform, not the Editor alone. A test A test class derives from ForgeTest, which makes a ForgeTestWorld before each test and audits and ends it after. A test is a [UnityTest] whose body runs through Live, from a frame's end: using System.Collections; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using FarEmerald.PlayForge.Testing; using NUnit.Framework; using UnityEngine.TestTools; public class BurnTests : ForgeTest { [UnityTest] public IEnumerator A_burn_ticks_twice_in_its_second([Values] Hub hub) => Live(async () => { var health = Make.Attribute("Health"); var target = World.Entity(hub, Make.Set(Make.Pool(health, 100f, 100f)), "Target"); var burn = Make.Effect("Burn", new EffectConfig { Policy = EEffectDurationPolicy.Durational, Target = health, Magnitude = -10f, Duration = 1f, PeriodicTicks = true, Ticks = 2, }); Assert.IsTrue(World.Hit(World.Entity(hub, name: "Source"), target, burn)); await Frames.Until(() => World.Value(target, health) <= 80f, 90, "its two ticks land"); Assert.AreEqual(80f, World.Value(target, health), 0.001f); }); } A test class whose tests need a base class of their own makes a world instead, and ends it, with await using: [UnityTest] public IEnumerator My_test() => UniTask.ToCoroutine(async () => { await using var world = await ForgeTestWorld.Start(); // ... the test, through world; then, if it wants the checks, await world.Audit() }); The world Entities: World.Entity(hub, set, name) makes an entity of an attribute set on either hub, Hub.Runtime (a RuntimeGameplayAbilitySystem) or Hub.Mono (a GameplayAbilitySystem on a GameObject of its own); World.FromIdentity(hub, identity) makes one from an identity asset, the game's own or one Make built, with its set, its starting abilities and items, and its sides. RuntimeEntity, MonoEntity and NewMonoEntity (made, not yet registered) make one hub's. Playing: World.Hit(source, target, effect) applies an effect, as a hit; World.Cast(caster, ability, target, level) gives an ability and asks it to start, as a player does, and Cast(caster, slot, target) starts the ability in a slot; World.Use(caster, ability, target) starts an ability the entity has already, as an item's; and World.Hold(holder, item, stacks) gives and equips an item. Each says whether it worked. Reading: World.Value(gas, attribute) and World.Base(gas, attribute), NaN where the entity hasn't it; World.Has(gas, effect) and World.Stacks(gas, effect); World.HasTag(gas, tag), a tag or one under it. Time: Frames.Step(n) runs whole frames, each Frames.DeltaTime long (1/60 of a second, or a class's DeltaTime) with one FixedUpdate; Frames.Seconds(s) as many as that time; Frames.Until(condition, within, what) steps until it holds, failing past within frames; ExactlyIn fails unless it holds exactly so many frames on; Holds fails if it stops holding. World.Clock(step) makes each frame take step seconds of PlayForge's own time (ForgeTime) instead. Chance: World.Rolls(0.1f, 0.9f) makes each roll come out as written, in turn and round again, and returns them, counting what's drawn (Drawn). A chance lands where it's above the roll: a roll of 0 always lands. Processes: World.Register(process) registers one the world ends if the test doesn't; World.Own(relay) makes it end one registered some other way; World.Template<T>(name) stands in for a prefab, and World.Spawn(template) registers it, returning the clone. Assets: Make builds them in code, destroyed with the world: Attribute, Element, Pool (between 0 and its base) and Stat, Set and UnusedSet, Identity and RuntimeIdentity, Effect (as an EffectConfig says: one impact, its duration and ticks, how another application stacks, its impact types, granted tags and workers), Item, Ability and Stage. Its tag names are unique in the world. The game's own assets are the test's to load. What must hold After each test that passed, the world's audit lets three frames settle, ends what the test left running of what it began, and fails the test where any of these broke: an entity's attribute parts don't sum to its value; what an entity dealt, read from its frame summaries, isn't what its targets received from it; a process is still running that the world didn't begin. The world checks the entities it makes; World.Observe(gas) adds one made elsewhere, as from a scene, and an entity made with observed: false is left out, as a test that measures allocation wants. A class whose tests leave processes running on purpose overrides Audits to false. Allocation AllocationProbe measures what's allocated, with the profiler's counter, as the GC's own reads 0 under Mono: Measure(action) what one run allocates, MeasureEach(action, runs, warmup) the mean of many after a warm-up, and await MeasureFrames(Frames, count) what whole frames allocate, the cleanest of up to three tries, as stray noise doesn't repeat and a leak does. Dispose it as the test ends. Traps Step frames; never call a process's update by hand. The world's ProcessControl steps what runs, as the game's does; calling an update yourself runs it out of order and hides what the frame does. A tag converts to text. NUnit's Does.Contain(tag) compares a list of tags as text and fails; check with World.HasTag, or Contains on the list itself. Unscaled time isn't stepped. Anything timed on Unity's unscaled time stays on the wall clock. One world at a time. ForgeTestWorld.Current is the one a test is in; PlayForge's static state is the world's while it lives, and the world gives back the clock and the rolls as it ends.

guides/VALUE_PIPELINES.html.title: Value Pipelines | PlayForge
guides/VALUE_PIPELINES.html.summary: Value Pipelines A Value Pipeline is an asset that takes a value as it lands, sends it through ordered stages, and gives what comes out. An effect's impact names one as its calculation, as an Unreal effect names its execution calculation: each hit of that impact goes through the pipeline's stages, so a project writes once how a hit's damage is worked out, and a new item that changes every hit is a stage, not an edit to each attack. It's generic: the value is any number an impact lands with, a blow, a heal, a drain. Create one from Create > PlayForge > Value Pipeline, or with New beside an impact's Pipeline field, which makes one named for the effect and uses it; once the field names one, Open shows it. A Crowd Control Rules or Effect Modifier field has the same two. Not a Scaler asset A Scaler asset is a number worked out from its context: a level table, × an attribute, a condition. A number field reads it wherever a number is read. A Value Pipeline transforms a value it's given. It runs once for each hit, as the hit lands, with the caster and the target both known, and its stages can do what a number can't: roll a chance once for the hit and keep it, route part of the value into a barrier, and say what each stage did. A stage's own numbers are number fields, so a stage reads × Attribute, conditions, curves and Scaler assets as any field does. When it runs It runs for what an impact commits: an instant impact's hit, and each tick of a periodic one. A lasting impact, as +10 Strength while a buff holds, is read again whenever its attribute changes, so a pipeline doesn't run it. A modifier's Change Impact brings a stage of its own (EFFECTS.md): a hit runs it after its pipeline, or alone where it has none, and the breakdown keeps it with the pipeline's steps; a lasting impact takes it on its magnitude. Stages Each stage has a Label, the name a breakdown gives it, and Enabled, which lets the value pass it by. Multiply: the value times a number read for the hit. A bonus, × the caster's Damage Amplification read as 1 + x; a reduction, × the target's Damage Resistance read as what's left; an armor curve; a bonus that reads the target, as 75% more while the target is above 90% of its health. Add: a number added to the value's size. A flat bonus of 10 makes a blow of −100 one of −110, and a heal of 50 one of 60. Chance: on a chance, the value times a number: a critical hit. It rolls once for the hit, and the breakdown notes it. Its Roll makes it pseudo-random or lucky (EFFECTS.md). Clamp: the value's size kept between two numbers, its sign as it was. Absorb: a loss taken first from another attribute of the one hit, as a barrier or a shield takes a blow before health. What it soaks comes off that attribute at the frame's end, and the rest goes on. An attribute with the Barrier role soaks the losses to the one it absorbs for with no stage at all (ATTRIBUTES.md). Block and Evade: a Chance, read as the effect lands, that stops it. Each rolls once, before anything of the effect lands, and where it comes up nothing of it does, its damage, tags, contained effects and on-hits, and its ticks aren't rolled again; the one hit hears Blocked or Evaded, and the dealer Hit Blocked or Hit Evaded. A defender brings one through an incoming modifier's Change Impact, as Tougher Times blocks the hits landing on its holder by a stacking curve of its stacks (EFFECTS.md). Its Stops says what it can stop: Losses, the default, an effect that lowers its attribute, an add below 0, a multiplier below 1 or an override below where it stands, so a heal lands past it unrolled; or Any Impact, heals and buffs too. As the hit commits, it passes the value on. Execute: a hit that would leave the one hit with less than its Share of its Attribute's base, the Health role's where it names none, takes the rest, as Culling Blade; the breakdown notes it. A project writes its own stage by deriving from AbstractValueStage and overriding Apply(value, in run). run.Context reads the hit's caster, target and level, as any number does, and run.Note notes what the stage did. A typical damage pipeline Amplification: Multiply by the caster's Damage Amplification (a Bonus Share, read as 1 + x). Critical: Chance, the caster's Crit Chance, × 2. Armor: Multiply by a curve of the target's Armor. Resistance: Multiply by the target's Damage Resistance (a Resistance, read as 1 − x). Barrier: Absorb into the target's Barrier. Every damage effect names it, so a blow of 100 from a caster with 50% amplification, on a target with 20% resistance, lands as 120. The Demo's blows go through two such pipelines, Physical Damage and Magic Damage in its Effects/Pipelines: each multiplies a blow by its dealer's Attack or Magic Amplification, a Stacking Curve of it read as 1 + it, then by what its target's Armor leaves, 100 ÷ (100 + Armor), or its Magic Resistance, 1 − it, kept between 0 and 1. Its Physical and Magic Strike templates name them, and so does each blow that takes one, so a new attack takes its kind's from its template. The breakdown An effect's spec keeps its last run as a Breakdown: the value in, each stage's before and after with its note, and the value out. spec.Breakdown.ToString() says it in a line: -100 → Amplification -150 → Resistance -120. A combat log, a debugger or a test reads it. Trying a pipeline A Value Pipeline's inspector has a Try section under its stages, which puts a value through them at each level of a range, as a Scaler asset's Try reads a scaler: Value In is the value a hit lands with, going in: a loss below 0, as a blow of 100 is −100, and a gain above. Chances Come Up settles each roll, so a try gives the same each time: on, each chance a stage rolls comes up where it can, a critical strike doubling the hit and a block stopping it; off, each misses where it can. A chance of 1 always comes up and one of 0 never does. Levels, 1 to 5 to start, are the hit's levels, for a stage whose number scales by level. Its Caster, Target and Caller are a Scaler asset's Try's: a row for each attribute a stage reads on a side, as a Multiply stage's Damage Amplification or an Absorb stage's Barrier, typed or filled from an Entity, and a row for each key a caller sets. Its Out row says what lands at each level. Click one to see its steps under the table: the value in, each stage's value in and out with its note, as "critical", and what comes out. A Block or Evade stage rolls first, as it does as an effect lands, and one that comes up stops the hit: nothing of it lands, and its level shows "—". No effect is behind a try, so what an Absorb stage soaks comes off no one, and a stage of your own that reads run.Carrier reads none. What's typed is kept for the session, never in the asset. ValuePipelineTry does the same in code, new ValuePipelineTry { Value = -100f }.Read(pipeline), and pipeline.Run(value, in context) puts a value through a pipeline against a number context of your own, with no effect behind it.

guides/WORKERS.html.title: PlayForge — Workers | PlayForge
guides/WORKERS.html.summary: PlayForge — Workers Workers are the small rules that react to what happens to an entity: a floor that keeps Health above 1, a share of each blow sent back, a rage at half Health, a burst as a tag comes off. This page maps each kind: when it runs, on whose system and for whom, and what its context holds. RECIPES.md builds common rules from them. Where workers come from An attribute set's Worker Group: the entity built from the set holds its workers as it lives. An entity's Worker Group (its Entity asset): the same, as the entity's own. Its project's Workers: every entity in a Forge Project holds the workers its settings list, under Workers in Project Settings → PlayForge, after its own, as it registers. A project starts with the Lifesteal worker, whose Share is yours to name. An item's, an ability's or an effect's Worker Group: the entity holds them while the item is equipped, the ability known, or the effect lasts on it. Two of an effect lasting give its group once. An effect's Workers: effect workers, which run for that effect's own events. Built in: an On Hit entry gives its holder an impact worker. Lifesteal The Lifesteal worker, an impact worker, heals its holder a share of each workable loss it deals another: the value of its holder's Share, the attribute it names, as 0.15 for 15%; with none it heals nothing. The losses that count are to its Receives attribute, and it heals its Heals attribute, each the Health role's where it names none, so a mana burn can heal Health. An effect raises the share while it should, as an effect has no lifesteal of its own. Only hits of the Impact Types it names count, as attacks; with none, any; so a second worker on another attribute, of spells' types, makes a spell vamp. A worker that runs once for a hit, as this one, runs once however many of it its holder has, its project's and its own: the first of the kind to take the hit. It allocates nothing, healing or not. The map Kind Hook When it runs For whom: its context's System What its context holds Attribute Pre Change Before a change to one of the entity's attributes lands: a commit, or a modifier registered or taken off The entity whose attribute changes WorkerContext: System, AttributeCache, Change (the incoming change: an Inline worker's edit is what commits, before bounds and rounding; a modifier's it only reads), FrameSummary, ActionQueue Attribute Post Change After the change lands The entity whose attribute changed The same, Change being what it changed by Impact Validate, then actions As a change the entity dealt lands on another's attribute, for the attribute the worker subscribes to The dealer; the one hit is ImpactData.Target ImpactWorkerContext: System (the dealer), ImpactData (Target, Attribute, the sourced change, RealImpact, OldValue), FrameSummary, ActionQueue Tag Activate, Tick, Resolve At the entity's end of frame: Activate as its tag requirements come to be met, Tick while they hold, Resolve as they no longer do. Read in a frame the entity's tags changed, or every frame where Evaluate Every Frame says The entity The system Analysis Analyze At the entity's end of frame, after its tag workers The entity The system and its FrameSummary: the frame's impacts dealt and received, by attribute, target and source; the effects applied and removed; the deaths Effect Application, Tick, Removal As the effect lands, at each of its execute ticks (with how many), and as it comes off The entity the effect is on EffectWorkerContext: System, Carrier (the effect's spec), FrameSummary, ActionQueue, ExecuteTicks; GetState<T>(worker) keeps what it counts for this application Effect Impact As a change the effect made lands The dealer, the effect's caster, not the one it's on; the one hit is ImpactData.Target The same, with ImpactData Inline or deferred. An attribute worker's Execution says how it acts. An Inline one runs inside the change, can edit the change in Pre Change, and must not change attributes itself, which would run workers inside workers. A Deferred one returns actions instead, as impact, analysis and effect workers do; the entity's action queue runs them at its end of frame, where they can change anything. A focused attribute worker, one that watches a single attribute, sets its Timing (Pre Change, Post Change or both), its Sign Policy (the changes it takes: losses, gains or either), and Allow Self Modification (whether it takes changes whose source and target are the same entity). The action queue What a deferred worker returns, and whatever else is queued to an entity (GetActionQueue().Enqueue), waits in the entity's action queue for its end of frame. When it runs. Four passes in each end of frame: the actions queued since the last; then those the tag workers' activations and resolutions queue; then those their ticks queue; then those the analysis workers, the Health watch and the effects' conditions queue. An action queued as a pass runs joins that pass. In what order. By priority, higher first (ActionPriority, from Critical's 100 down to Cleanup's −300), and in the order queued within one. Enqueue(action, priorityOverride) puts one at another priority. What's heard. Each action is heard as it's queued (OnActionQueued), then once more as it's done with: run (OnActionExecuted); dropped unrun (OnActionInvalidated): its IsValid said no as its turn came, it was taken off, or its entity had ended; failed (OnActionFailed, with what it threw): its IsValid or its Execute threw. It's written to the Console as well, and the rest of the queue runs on. The queue's events and the entity's callbacks both tell them. The frame's summary keeps the dropped and the failed, and an EffectJournal settles a worker's action as Ran, Dropped or Failed. Taken off. Remove(action) takes one off, RemoveWhere(match) every one it picks, and Clear() all of them, each heard as dropped; the rest keep their order. An entity that ends. Its queue closes (IsClosed): what waited is dropped and heard, and an action queued to it after is dropped at once, so nothing waits on it for good. Another entity's queue. An action queued to another entity runs at that entity's end of frame: this frame if its end of frame is still to come, by the order the entities step in, or else the next. The guard. A pass runs 10,000 actions at most, so an action that queues another for good can't hold the frame. Those left past it wait for the next pass, and the queue writes an error. Hearing workers run An entity tells its workers' runs to whoever listens to its callbacks, and to no one else, so a worker no one hears costs nothing more: OnEffectWorkerRan: one of its effects' workers heard one of the effect's moments, its Hook (Application, Tick, Removal or Impact), on its Side (the Target, or the Dealer for a hit, as the map says), with the System it ran on and the actions it Queued. A tick, which its workers hear every frame, is told only as one executes or a worker queues something. OnImpactWorkerRan: one of its impact workers ran for a hit it dealt, with its Execution and what it queued. OnAttributeChangeStep: a step a change to one of its attributes took, an attribute worker's, with its Timing, its Execution, the change Before and After and what it Queued; a barrier's soak; or a gain's scaling. The combat log keeps each hit's steps (ENTITIES.md). An EffectJournal hears all of it for the entities it's given (ENTITIES.md). Workable and unworkable A change is workable unless it says it isn't (SourcedModifiedAttributeValue.ImpactIsWorkable). An unworkable one is a change the system makes on its own account (GenerateUnworkable), as the pulse each attribute starts with, or a transfer's two sides. Only a workable change: reaches impact workers, unless a worker's Accept Unworkable Impact is on; is soaked by a barrier as a loss, and scaled by its attribute's Gains Scaled By as a gain, as Healing Received; sends the core's Impact Dealt and Impact Taken events, and counts toward the kill: the killer is whoever dealt the last workable loss to the Health role's attribute; counts for lifesteal, and is returned by Return Damage; is written in the combat log as a hit, taken or dealt; another is a Change. Attribute workers run for every change, workable or not; one that cares reads ctx.Change.Value.ImpactIsWorkable. Traps An impact worker runs for the dealer. Its context's System is the dealer, and the one hit is ImpactData.Target. A worker that took System for the one hit applied its holder's effects to the target, and read the target's items for its holder's. An effect worker's Impact hook runs on the dealer's side too. Its System is the effect's caster, where its Application, Tick and Removal hooks' System is the one the effect is on. A stacking effect's periodic tick lands once for each stack, while its lasting change counts once. A number that reads the effect's stacks on each tick multiplies again: Hangover, which read its stacks, took 100 a tick where 20 was meant. Read the stacks in a lasting change, or leave them out of a periodic one. The Problems view warns of it. What a worker sets in motion waits for the frame's end. Deferred actions, deaths and the kills they give, and an aura's effect coming off a dead holder all land at the entity's end of frame, so one area's hits resolve together (EFFECTS.md).

index.html.title: PlayForge | PlayForge
index.html.summary: PlayForge PlayForge is a gameplay framework for Unity 6, modelled on Unreal's Gameplay Ability System. Every ability, effect, attribute, tag and item is an asset you build in the inspector, and one hub on each entity runs them all. Start here Getting Started sets PlayForge up in a project, makes an entity, and gives it an ability that changes an attribute through an effect. The guides Area Guides Gameplay Entities · Attributes · Attribute Sets · Effects · Effect & Attribute Pipeline · Value Pipelines · Scalers · Abilities · Items · Cues · Workers Running it Processes · Task Sequences · Saving and Loading · Spreadsheets Tools The Creator Lab · Testing Your Content Recipes Recipes: common rules built from PlayForge's own assets, field by field These guides are the ones the package ships in PlayForge/Documentation, and each help button in PlayForge's inspectors opens its section here.
